Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The growing use of duplex stainless steels (DSSs) has spurred extensive research and development, particularly concerning weldability challenges. The increasing interest in additive manufacturing (AM) using directed energy deposition (DED) has further highlighted the need for precise sample preparation to ensure accurate microstructural characterization. This paper consolidates best practices for preparing samples to effectively reveal microstructures and secondary phases in DSSs. By optimizing polishing techniques and etching methods, the work provides guidelines for distinguishing ferrite and austenite across the base material, heat-affected zone (HAZ), and weld metal, while also enabling the detection of intermetallic phases and discrete secondary precipitates. Examples of typical deviations, etching phenomena, and potential pitfalls are also provided. The preparation strategies presented are tailored to support subsequent analysis using light optical microscopy (LOM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Oxidation reactions on semiconducting metal oxide (SMOs) surfaces have been extensively worked on in catalysis, fuel cells, and sensors. SMOs engage powerfully in energy-related applications such as batteries, supercapacitors, solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs), and sensors. A deep understanding of SMO surface and oxygen interactions and defect engineering has become significant because all of the above-mentioned applications are based on the adsorption/absorption and consumption/transportation of adsorbed (physisorbed-chemisorbed) oxygen. More understanding of adsorbed oxygen and oxygen vacancies (VO•,VO••) is needed, as the former is the vital requirement for sensing chemical reactions, while the latter facilitates the replenishment of adsorbed oxygen ions on the surface. We determined the relation between sensor response (sensitivity) and the amounts of adsorbed oxygen ions (O2(ads)−, O(ads), −O2(ads)2−, O(ads)2−), water/hydroxide groups (H2O/OH−), oxygen vacancies (VO•, VO••), and ordinary lattice oxygen ions (Olattice2−) as a function of temperature. During hydrogen (H2) testing, the different oxidation states (W6+, W5+, and W4+) of WO3 were quantified and correlated with oxygen vacancy formation (VO•, VO••). We used a combined application of XPS, UPS, XPEEM-LEEM, and chemical, electrical, and sensory analysis for H2 sensing. The sensor response was extraordinarily high: 424 against H2 at a temperature of 250 °C was recorded and explained on the basis of defect engineering, including oxygen vacancies and chemisorbed oxygen ions and surface stoichiometry of WO3. We established a correlation between the H2 sensing mechanism of WO3, sensor signal magnitude, the amount of adsorbed oxygen ions, and sensor testing temperature. This paper also provides a review of the detection, quantification, and identification of different adsorbed oxygen species. The different surface and bulk-sensitive characterization techniques relevant to analyzing the SMOs-based sensor are tabulated, providing the sensor designer with the chemical, physical, and electronic information extracted from each technique.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This work introduces an additive direct-write nanofabrication technique for producing extremely conductive gold nanostructures from a commercial metalorganic precursor. Gold content of 91 atomic % (at. %) was achieved by using water as an oxidative enhancer during direct-write deposition. A model was developed based on the deposition rate and the chemical composition and it explains the surface processes that lead to the increases in gold purity and deposition yield. Co-injection of an oxidative enhancer enabled Focused Electron Beam Induced Deposition (FEBID)—a maskless, resistless deposition method for three dimensional (3D) nanostructures—to directly yield pure gold in a single process step, without post-deposition purification. Gold nanowires displayed resistivity down to 8.8 μΩ cm. This is the highest conductivity achieved so far from FEBID and it opens the possibility of applications in nanoelectronics, such as direct-write contacts to nanomaterials. The increased gold deposition yield and the ultralow carbon level will facilitate future applications such as the fabrication of 3D nanostructures in nanoplasmonics and biomolecule immobilization.

Abstract:
A set of ancient Antoninianus silver coins, dating back between 249 and 274 A.D. and minted in Rome, Galliae, Orient and Ticinum, have been characterized. We use, for the first time, a combination of nano-invasive (focused ion beam-field emission scanning electron microscopy-X-ray microanalysis (FIB-FESEM-EDX), voltammetry of microparticles (VIMP)) and destructive techniques (scanning electron microscopy (SEM-EDX) and electron microprobe analysis (EMPA)) along with non-invasive, i.e., micro-Raman spectroscopy. The results revealed that, contrary to the extended belief, a complex Ag-Cu-Pb-Sn alloy was used. The use of alloys was common in the flourishing years of the Roman Empire. In the prosperous periods, Romans produced Ag-Cu alloys with relatively high silver content for the manufacture of both the external layers and inner nucleus of coins. This study also revealed that, although surface silvering processes were applied in different periods of crisis under the reign of Antoninii, even during crisis, Romans produced Antoninianus of high quality. Moreover, a first attempt to improve the silvering procedure using Hg-Ag amalgam has been identified.

Abstract:
Five-component icosahedral quasicrystals with compositions in the range Al68–73Fe11–16Cu10–12Cr1–4Ni1–2 were recently recovered after shocking metallic CuAl5 and (Mg0.75Fe0.25)2SiO4 olivine in a stainless steel 304 chamber, intended to replicate a natural shock that affected the Khatyrka meteorite. The iron in those quasicrystals might have originated either from reduction of Fe2+ in olivine or from the stainless steel chamber. In this study, we clarify the shock synthesis mechanism of icosahedral quasicrystals through two new shock recovery experiments. When CuAl5 and Fe2+-bearing olivine were isolated in a Ta capsule, no quasicrystals were found. However, with only metallic starting materials, numerous micron-sized five-component icosahedral quasicrystals, average composition Al72Cu12Fe12Cr3Ni1, were found at the interface between CuAl5 and stainless steel, demonstrating nucleation of quasicrystals under shock without any redox reaction. We present detailed characterization of recovered quasicrystals and discuss possible mechanisms for generating sufficiently high temperatures to reach melting with relatively weak shocks. We discuss the implications of our five-component quasicrystal for the stability of quasicrystals, which have previously only been considered in alloy systems with four or fewer components. Even small amounts of additional metals expand the stability range of the icosahedral phase and facilitate routine syntheses without extraordinary precision in preparation of starting mixtures.

From text 'newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 1-2'.

Dale E. Newbury. Quantitative electron probe microanalysis of rough targets: testing the peak-to-local background method. Scanning, 26 3:103-14, Dec 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950260302, doi:10.1002/sca.4950260302. This article has 24 citations.

This excerpt establishes that conventional quantitative EPMA/SEM-EDS matrix-correction procedures are fundamentally intended for polished, flat, homogeneous bulk specimens measured against standards under the same geometry. Their analytical performance depends on composition being the only source of intensity differences; surface roughness, relief, particle dimensions, or other geometric differences between standards and unknowns violate that requirement. Geometry becomes especially problematic when specimen features or objects approach the micrometer-scale electron/x-ray interaction volume, because electron scattering, x-ray generation, and absorption path lengths differ from the flat-target assumptions. Thus, particles embedded in epoxy cannot automatically be treated as bulk standards: their dimensions must be sufficiently large relative to the interaction volume, and measurements near particle edges or epoxy boundaries are vulnerable to escape, substrate, and absorption effects. The excerpt does not provide a numerical particle-size threshold or a specific 15–20 keV calculation, but it supports the principle that edge and finite-size effects must be avoided or modeled. Reorientation can reduce effects, while the peak-to-local-background method can provide corrections for rough or geometrically compromised targets.

From text 'newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 3-4'.

Dale E. Newbury. Quantitative electron probe microanalysis of rough targets: testing the peak-to-local background method. Scanning, 26 3:103-14, Dec 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950260302, doi:10.1002/sca.4950260302. This article has 24 citations.

The excerpt establishes that polished, homogeneous, conducting bulk standards are the appropriate baseline for quantitative EPMA/SEM-EDS roughness studies because their composition is uniform and their flat geometry minimizes uncontrolled topographic and charging effects. It also emphasizes that SEM images can make highly irregular specimens appear readily examinable even when their geometry is unsuitable for quantitative x-ray analysis. Surface relief changes both the primary-electron interaction and the x-ray absorption path length, so measured intensities can be substantially modified by geometry; these effects are particularly strong for low-energy lines, although absorption changes occur at all photon energies. The particle experiments used spherical alloy particles 20–200 µm in diameter—explicitly much larger than the flat-surface interaction volume—and compared them with polished cross sections analyzed using ZAF corrections. Thus, conventional bulk matrix corrections derived for flat polished material cannot by themselves remove particle-shape, edge, shadowing, or variable-path-length effects. The excerpt documents measurements at 20 keV and indicates that high-energy lines are less sensitive than low-energy lines, but it does not specifically discuss epoxy mounting, nor does it provide a complete quantitative threshold for edge effects at 15–20 keV. Particle dimensions relative to the interaction volume and geometry must therefore be evaluated explicitly.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 4-5'.

Dale E. Newbury. Quantitative electron probe microanalysis of rough targets: testing the peak-to-local background method. Scanning, 26 3:103-14, Dec 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950260302, doi:10.1002/sca.4950260302. This article has 24 citations.

The excerpt establishes that polished cross sections or flat bulk surfaces provide the reference analyses for quantitative EPMA, using conventional ZAF matrix corrections and pure-element standards. For particles, geometry must be considered in relation to the electron interaction volume: an approximately 80 µm spherical particle is treated as effectively flat at its top center when its curvature is much larger than the interaction volume. At other positions, particle curvature changes the x-ray take-off angle and absorption path. At 20 keV, moving toward the EDS raises the low-energy (<4 keV) intensity because the take-off angle increases and absorption decreases, whereas moving away from the EDS produces strong low-energy attenuation as x-rays traverse more particle material. The high-energy (>4 keV) portion is comparatively insensitive to these added paths. Conventional ZAF results therefore can show geometry-driven errors, especially for low-energy lines: a backside position produced an anomalously low analytical total (Σ = 0.834), while a toward-EDS position gave Σ = 1.037. Normalized concentrations may substantially misrepresent low-energy elements when they are absorbed. The excerpt does not specifically establish epoxy-mounting requirements or a universal particle-size threshold; it supports comparing embedded-particle results with polished-section standards and ensuring particle dimensions/curvature exceed the interaction-volume scale where a flat-surface approximation is intended.

This excerpt establishes that accurate quantitative EPMA is best performed on a homogeneous, polished, flat bulk standard or specimen. The analyzed volume must be compositionally uniform throughout the electron- and x-ray-excited region; layered or heterogeneous materials require additional measurements and correction procedures. Surface preparation is important because local tilt, scratches, ridges, and trenches alter both x-ray generation and absorption path length. The cited polishing work indicates that an optical-quality surface, with scratches below 100 nm amplitude, may be required to eliminate topography effects, especially for strongly absorbed soft x-rays. At 20 keV, roughness on the order of 1–5 µm is comparable to the electron interaction volume and can therefore produce major intensity variations. The results show particularly strong changes in low-energy lines, while spectra become much more stable above 6 keV. The excerpt does not directly establish quantitative requirements for particles embedded in epoxy, nor does it provide a specific allowable particle diameter or a dedicated 15-keV edge-effect measurement. However, its interaction-volume and path-length discussion implies that particles should be sufficiently large and geometrically isolated to contain the excited volume and avoid epoxy contribution, surface relief, and particle-edge absorption/shadowing. Small particles or measurements near edges would violate the flat, homogeneous geometry assumed for bulk standards and require explicit geometric or matrix corrections.

This excerpt establishes that quantitative EPMA/SEM-EDS is intrinsically most reliable for homogeneous, metallographically polished bulk surfaces, whereas rough or finite particles introduce substantial geometry-dependent errors. The relevant effects include variable absorption paths between the excited volume and the EDS detector, electron scattering from tilted surfaces, remote excitation of characteristic X-rays, and the detector’s broad acceptance angle. The example of a 50 µm IN100 particle measured at 20 kV/0.5 nA demonstrates extreme absorption at a position away from the detector; the low-energy spectrum can lose substantial intensity, and raw or normalized concentrations are markedly improved by peak-to-background correction, though residual errors remain. The text also notes that the required micrometer-scale homogeneity is satisfied by only a limited set of conducting metallic materials, motivating roughened reference alloys and spectra recorded under multiple scanning geometries. Thus, particle size and position relative to the interaction volume cannot be treated as irrelevant: finite particles, edges, curvature, and detector-facing versus detector-opposed locations alter excitation and absorption. However, this excerpt does not explicitly quantify the particle-dimension-to-interaction-volume criterion or discuss epoxy embedding directly; those requirements would need support from other portions of the literature.

The excerpt establishes that quantitative EPMA/SEM-EDS is strongly dependent on specimen geometry, detector visibility, and the relationship between the electron beam, analyzed surface, and EDS takeoff path. It does not specifically provide particle-size criteria, interaction-volume dimensions, or a direct comparison between polished bulk standards and particles embedded in epoxy. For polished, flat bulk standards, the geometry is comparatively controlled, but detector and instrument configuration can still introduce backscatter and rescattering effects. For rough, tilted, recessed, or particle-like specimens, surrounding topography can block characteristic x-rays, increase absorption, and produce remote excitation: backscattered electrons may strike adjacent regions and generate nonlocalized x-rays that appear as trace, minor, or major constituents. The recommended mitigation is careful reorientation, preferably with the beam normal to the surface and the feature on the detector-facing side; however, low-angle or recessed regions can still contribute spurious signal. The passage therefore supports treating embedded particles as geometrically non-ideal targets and warns that standards must reproduce relevant excitation and detection geometry where possible. It does not establish a numerical requirement that particles exceed the interaction volume, nor does it quantify edge effects specifically at 15–20 keV. It does describe peak-to-local-background ratios as an internal monitor for geometry-related changes.

Abstract:
Abstract Fluorine and chlorine X‑ray count rates are known to vary significantly during electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) of apatite. Since the rate, timing, and magnitude of this variation are a function of apatite orientation and composition, as well as EPMA operating conditions, this represents a significant problem for volatile element analysis in apatite. Although the effect is thought to be an intrinsic crystallographic response to electron-beam exposure, the mechanisms and causes of the count rate variability remain unclear. We tackle this by examining directly the effects of electron-beam exposure on apatite, by performing secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) depth profiles of points previously subject to electron-beam irradiation. During irradiation of fluorapatite, oriented with the c-axis parallel to the electron beam, halogens become progressively concentrated at the sample surface, even under a relatively low power (15 nA, 10-15 kV) beam. This surface enrichment corresponds to an observed increase in EPMA FKa X‑ray count rates. After prolonged irradiation, the surface region starts to lose halogens and becomes progressively depleted, corresponding with a drop in EPMA count rates. Under normal EPMA operating conditions there is no halogen redistribution in fluorapatite oriented with the c-axis perpendicular to the electron beam, or in chlorapatite. We infer that anionic enrichment results from the migration of halogens away from a center of charge build-up caused by the implantation of electrons from the EPMA beam, assisted by the thermal gradient induced by electron-matter interactions. The process of surface enrichment is best explained by halogen migration through interstitial crystallographic sites in the c-axis channel. This suggests that once the thermal and electric fields are removed, halogens may relax back to their original positions on very long timescales or with sample heating.

## pqac-00000008

From text 'remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 7-9'.

G. Rémond, C. Nockolds, M. Phillips, and C. Roques-carmes. Implications of polishing techniques in quantitative x-ray microanalysis. Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 107:639-662, Nov 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.052, doi:10.6028/jres.107.052. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies several polishing artifacts that can compromise quantitative X-ray microanalysis. Final polishing is intended to remove residual scratches, polishing-generated surface compounds, and the damaged surface layer; if these remain, precipitates and phases may be concealed and measured X-ray intensities may not represent the underlying material. Hard cloths can produce a severely damaged surface, while abrasive wear can round specimen edges, degrading geometrical accuracy and edge-sensitive measurements. Chemical-mechanical polishing of metals forms an oxide layer that is progressively removed, so residual oxide or altered surface chemistry may be significant. Colloidal-silica polishing can create scratches if the pad is not renewed or kept wet, including damage from silica crystallization. The substrate and abrasive mode strongly affect topography: loose abrasive wear produces ploughing and crater-rich surfaces, whereas bound abrasives produce cutting scratches. Differential wear between minerals of different hardness creates steps or relief at interfaces; arsenopyrite wears more rapidly than quartz in the example. Such roughness, craters, scratches, relief, and damaged layers can alter interaction volumes and X-ray escape, especially at phase boundaries and in softer phases. The excerpt does not specifically document contamination, porosity, or smearing.

This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies several polishing-induced artifacts that can compromise quantitative X-ray microanalysis. Mechanical polishing of metals can produce rapid surface oxidation, with oxide layers ranging from a few nanometers to hundreds of nanometers; thermal effects, friction, and electrochemical charging during abrasion accelerate these reactions. In sulfide minerals, polishing can cause sulfur volatilization and formation of metal oxides. Contamination may be transferred from neighboring phases: wear debris can smear matrix material over inclusions, while silver-bearing surface compounds can form or evolve after polishing through light, heat, decomposition, and diffusion. Polishing also leaves a structurally damaged subsurface zone, especially in polycrystalline metals, involving strain hardening, crystallographic preferred orientation, and possible grain-boundary de-cohesion. Repeated finer-abrasive steps reduce earlier damage but introduce new damage, so a thin altered layer may remain undetectable optically. The text further notes layered surface contaminants and continuous composition gradients with depth, both of which can bias measured X-ray intensities. Although not all requested artifact categories are discussed in this excerpt, it directly supports chemical alteration, contamination, smearing, and mechanical deformation/damage as important sources of quantitative-analysis error.

The excerpt specifically documents roughness and topographic artifacts produced by abrading a polished metal standard. Surface geometry changes both the primary-electron interaction and the X-ray absorption path length, causing substantial intensity variations even when the bulk composition is homogeneous. These effects are strongest for low-energy lines, such as Cu-Lα and Au-Mα, although roughness-related absorption changes affect photons at all energies. High-energy Cu-Kα is comparatively insensitive, with an expected variation of about 2% for micrometer-scale features, and can function as an internal reference for evaluating low-energy distortions. Point analyses on the rough Cu–Au alloy produced Cu-L/Cu-K relative errors ranging from −92% to +42%, far exceeding ordinary counting and deconvolution uncertainty. Scanning larger areas reduces random variation but does not necessarily remove systematic bias: the largest scan showed Cu-L intensity approximately 20% below the ideal and Cu-K approximately 6% below it. The excerpt does not provide evidence about polishing-induced chemical contamination, deformation, edge rounding, porosity, relief, or smearing; its demonstrated concern is geometric roughness/topography and the resulting absorption and excitation artifacts in quantitative X-ray analysis of metals.

In chalcopyrite, polishing produces surface contamination by carbon-, oxygen-, and silver-bearing compounds, while abrasive carriers and subsequent polishing can mechanically remove or dissolve pre-existing surface layers. Polishing also modifies iron-oxide and copper-rich layers, changing surface reflectivity and indicating chemical alteration of the analyzed surface. After exposure to air, polished chalcopyrite develops thicker oxidized layers and colored regions, particularly around holes or fissures; these evolving surface films can alter measured composition and signal generation. For ZnS, mechanical polishing with diamond or alumina can create an amorphous or heavily damaged near-surface layer, whereas CMP better preserves crystallographic information. Mechanical polishing and indentation also alter hardness, produce fissures and grain-boundary revelation, and generate lattice disorder and deep subsurface strain fields. Such damaged, chemically altered, contaminated, or strained volumes can yield analyses that do not represent the underlying bulk. Mineral Characterization Using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM): A Review of the Fundamentals, Advancements, and Research Directions Valid Text Names: 'ali2023mineralcharacterizationusing pages 1-6', 'ali2023mineralcharacterizationusing pages 6-10', 'ali2023mineralcharacterizationusing pages 10-16', 'ali2023mineralcharacterizationusing pages 16-16' BibTex: @article{ali2023mineralcharacterizationusing, author = "Ali, Asif and Zhang, Ning and Santos, Rafael M.", title = "Mineral Characterization Using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM): A Review of the Fundamentals, Advancements, and Research Directions", year = "2023", journal = "Applied Sciences", month = "Nov", doi = "10.20944/preprints202310.2059.v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202310.2059.v1", volume = "13", pages = "12600", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "23", issn = "2076-3417" } Abstract: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is a powerful tool in the domains of materials science, mining, and geology owing to its enormous potential to provide unique insight into micro and nanoscale worlds. This comprehensive review discusses the background development of SEM, basic SEM operation, including specimen preparation and image processing, and the fundamental theoretical calculations underlying SEM operation. It provides a foundational understanding for engineers and scientists who have never had a chance to dig in depth into SEM, contributing to their understanding of the workings and development of this robust analytical technique. The present review covers how SEM serves as a crucial tool in mineral characterization, with specific discussion on the workings and research fronts of SEM-EDX, SEM-AM, SEM-MLA, and QEMSCAN. With automation gaining pace in the development of all spheres of technology, understanding the uncertainties in SEM measurements is very important. The constraints in mineral phase identification by EDS spectra and sample preparation are conferred. In the end, future research directions for SEM are analyzed with the possible incorporation of machine learning, deep learning, and artificial intelligence tools to automate the process of mineral identification, quantification, and efficient communication with researchers so that the robustness and objectivity of the analytical process can be improved and the analysis time and involved costs can be reduced. This review also discusses the idea of integrating robotics with SEM to make the equipment portable so that further mineral characterization insight can be gained not only on Earth but also on other terrestrial grounds. Abstract:
Electron-excited X-ray microanalysis performed in the scanning electron microscope with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) is a core technique for characterization of the microstructure of materials. The recent advances in EDS performance with the silicon drift detector (SDD) enable accuracy and precision equivalent to that of the high spectral resolution wavelength-dispersive spectrometer employed on the electron probe microanalyzer platform. SDD-EDS throughput, resolution, and stability provide practical operating conditions for measurement of high-count spectra that form the basis for peak fitting procedures that recover the characteristic peak intensities even for elemental combination where severe peak overlaps occur, such PbS, MoS2, BaTiO3, SrWO4, and WSi2. Accurate analyses are also demonstrated for interferences involving large concentration ratios: a major constituent on a minor constituent (Ba at 0.4299 mass fraction on Ti at 0.0180) and a major constituent on a trace constituent (Ba at 0.2194 on Ce at 0.00407; Si at 0.1145 on Ta at 0.0041). Accurate analyses of low atomic number elements, C, N, O, and F, are demonstrated. Measurement of trace constituents with limits of detection below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm) is possible within a practical measurement time of 500 s.

## pqac-00000016

From text 'humphreys2006simsinvestigationof pages 7-8'.

M. C.S. Humphreys, S. L. Kearns, and J. D. Blundy. Sims investigation of electron-beam damage to hydrous, rhyolitic glasses: implications for melt inclusion analysis. American Mineralogist, 91:667-679, Apr 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.2138/am.2006.1936, doi:10.2138/am.2006.1936. This article has 138 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt gives the Kanaya–Okayama electron range relation as RKO (µm) = 0.0276 A E0^1.67/(Z ρ^0.89), where A is atomic mass in g/mol, Z is atomic number, ρ is density in g/cm³, and E0 is beam energy in keV. This range estimates electron penetration depth in the specimen. For the hydrous rhyolitic glasses discussed, calculated penetration depths were provided for 15, 20, and 25 keV, but the numerical values from Table 2 are not included in the excerpt. The text states that alkali-ion migration depth is less than electron penetration depth and less than the depth of maximum implanted electron density. Monte Carlo simulations further indicate that increasing accelerating voltage from 15 to 20 keV increases both penetration depth and the depth of the charge center, while also increasing the maximum dimension of the electron-irradiated interaction volume. Thus, specimen or particle dimensions should exceed the relevant penetration/interaction-volume dimensions to avoid electron-beam effects extending through the entire material. However, this excerpt does not state explicit minimum specimen or particle dimensions at 15–20 keV; those would require the missing Table 2 values or calculation using the equation and the specimen composition and density.

## pqac-00000017

From text 'newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 2-3'.

Dale E. Newbury. Quantitative electron probe microanalysis of rough targets: testing the peak-to-local background method. Scanning, 26 3:103-14, Dec 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950260302, doi:10.1002/sca.4950260302. This article has 24 citations.

The excerpt does not provide the Kanaya–Okayama range equation, so the equation cannot be extracted from these pages. It does provide a relevant numerical scale: for a 20 keV electron beam, the electron interaction volume is described as being comparable to surface-topography dimensions of approximately 1–5 µm. This indicates that specimen roughness or particle dimensions on the order of a few micrometres can substantially affect quantitative EPMA because they modify electron-excited volume and x-ray absorption paths. The text also states that quantitative interpretation assumes the specimen is homogeneous throughout the complete electron- and x-ray-excited volume. Layered or compositionally heterogeneous specimens require measurements at multiple beam energies and more elaborate correction procedures. For accurate analysis, surface topography should generally be removed by grinding and polishing; the cited preparation study found that an optical-quality finish, with scratches below 100 nm, was needed to fully eliminate topography effects for strongly absorbed x-rays. Thus, the excerpt supports a conceptual minimum-dimension guideline of several micrometres at 20 keV, but it does not give a specific particle-size threshold at 15 keV or the numerical Kanaya–Okayama calculation.

The excerpt identifies the Kanaya–Okayama (KO) range as the method used to calculate the electron penetration depth, denoted ds, and includes a table comparing acoustic-wave-source parameters for 5 MHz and 1.3 GHz chopped electron beams. However, the actual Kanaya–Okayama range equation, its material-dependent constants, and numerical penetration-depth values are not present in the supplied pages. The excerpt also does not provide a calculation specifically at 15–20 keV or explicitly convert the interaction volume into a minimum specimen or particle dimension. Conceptually, the relevant guidance is that electron penetration and the resulting interaction region determine the depth and lateral scale over which energy is deposited; this scale must be considered when selecting specimen dimensions or interpreting signals from small particles. The document compares KO-range estimates with Monte Carlo simulations for silicon and illustrates electron interaction profiles, while a separate figure concerns PMMA etching. The simulation used 104 electron trajectories and a 5 nm beam width, whereas the table assumes a 50 nm beam size. These details support qualitative discussion of interaction-volume dimensions, but the excerpt alone is insufficient to extract a numerical minimum particle/specimen size at 15–20 keV.

The excerpt does not provide the Kanaya–Okayama electron-range equation or a numerical evaluation specifically at 15–20 keV. It does, however, give conceptual and dimensional guidance relevant to selecting specimen or particle size. Bulk specimens should be sufficiently large to contain the electron-excited X-ray generation region, stated as typically 0.5–10 μm, and also the larger region associated with secondary X-ray fluorescence, typically 10–100 μm. For conventional SEM/EDS k-ratio/matrix-correction analysis, the material must be compositionally homogeneous throughout the volume contributing primary characteristic X-rays and secondary fluorescence. Thus, particles or specimens smaller than the relevant interaction or fluorescence dimensions may violate the bulk-specimen assumptions and require geometry-specific treatment. The excerpt also emphasizes that surface condition matters: roughness, scratches, pits, implantation, or differential sputtering can alter electron penetration and X-ray absorption paths. These ranges are general values rather than an explicit 15–20 keV calculation; the surrounding chapter’s contents indicate that beam energy is selected as an instrumentation parameter, but the supplied pages do not connect a particular Kanaya–Okayama range to 15 or 20 keV.

G Valdrè, D Moro, and G Ulian. Correction factors for the effect of shape and thickness of sem-eds microanalysis of asbestos fibres by monte carlo simulation. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt does not contain the Kanaya–Okayama electron range equation, nor does it provide a numerical penetration depth or an explicit rule linking electron interaction volume to the minimum specimen or particle dimensions at 15–20 keV. It does, however, identify numerical simulations at 15 keV for asbestos-fibre bundles with square cross sections and several listed thicknesses, from 0.1 mm to 2.0 mm. The accompanying table reports element-specific k-ratios for crocidolite, amosite, tremolite-asbestos, chrysotile, anthophyllite-asbestos, and actinolite-asbestos. In general, the tabulated k-ratios decline substantially as the listed fibre thickness decreases, indicating that finite thickness and geometry strongly affect EDS results. For example, crocidolite Si Kα changes from 1.01 at 2.0 mm to 0.07 at 0.1 mm, while chrysotile Si Kα changes from 1.02 to 0.05 over the same listed range. These data demonstrate thickness-dependent interaction/escape effects but do not establish a Kanaya–Okayama range or a minimum dimension criterion. The excerpt also references Monte Carlo work on the effect of asbestos bundle and fibre shape and thickness, but the relevant equation and penetration-volume discussion must be obtained from the cited full paper or another portion of the source.

## pqac-00000021

From text 'carpenter2008epmastandardsthe pages 1-2'.

PK Carpenter. Epma standards: the good, the bad, and the ugly. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 14:530-531, Aug 2008. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927608088740, doi:10.1017/s1431927608088740. This article has 17 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not specifically discuss whether grains or fragments embedded in epoxy are acceptable, nor does it identify epoxy mounting itself as a problem. It does, however, state the general quality criteria expected for EPMA standards: they should be homogeneous at the micron scale, well characterized, widely available, and compositionally similar to the samples being analyzed. Small master fragments are viewed as problematic because they generally cannot be independently characterized by techniques other than EPMA; their working compositions therefore depend on the accuracy of the microprobe analysis. The excerpt contrasts preferred large fragments with small grains, noting that commercial mounts should be produced from large fragments from well-stocked standard-material supplies, since users prefer approximately 1 mm chunks rather than 10 µm grains. Grain size alone is therefore not the sole acceptance criterion: a small grain could be usable if it is demonstrably homogeneous and well characterized, but undocumented origin, assumed composition, EPMA-only calibration, or multiphase intergrowth makes a standard deficient. The text also warns that multiphase or heterogeneous materials are unsuitable and emphasizes independent analytical pedigree, such as wet chemistry or NIST-related characterization.

## pqac-00000022

From text 'newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 2-4'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Performing elemental microanalysis with high accuracy and high precision by scanning electron microscopy/silicon drift detector energy-dispersive x-ray spectrometry (sem/sdd-eds). Journal of Materials Science, 50:493-518, Nov 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2, doi:10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2. This article has 630 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

High-accuracy SEM-EDS k-ratio/matrix correction requires standards and unknowns to be measured under closely matched conditions: highly polished, unetched surfaces; the same beam energy, delivered dose (beam current and detector live time), beam-incidence angle, detector take-off angle, detector efficiency, and effectively constant detector-to-target geometry/solid angle. Surface topography is especially damaging for low-energy X-rays, so flat, smooth, metallographically prepared specimens are essential. The excerpt does not state a specific bulk-dimension requirement, but it emphasizes reproducible specimen positioning and warns that specimen geometry can severely affect accuracy regardless of whether standards-based or standardless analysis is used. Standards and analyzed regions should represent homogeneous material at the micrometer scale; the cited materials included specimens confirmed homogeneous laterally on that scale. Under suitable conditions and without significant peak overlap, Si(Li)-EDS achieved approximately -1.6% to +1.0% relative error for Cu-Au standards, comparable to WDS performance. The broader WDS benchmark had a 2.5% relative standard deviation, with about 95% of results within ±5% relative error. Violating polish, geometry, matching conditions, or homogeneity can therefore move results outside this accuracy range, while peak overlaps and incorrect qualitative identification further undermine quantitative reliability.

## pqac-00000023

From text 'newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 11-13'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Performing elemental microanalysis with high accuracy and high precision by scanning electron microscopy/silicon drift detector energy-dispersive x-ray spectrometry (sem/sdd-eds). Journal of Materials Science, 50:493-518, Nov 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2, doi:10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2. This article has 630 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a rigorous SEM/SDD-EDS k-ratio protocol modeled on EPMA/WDS practice. Specimens should have highly polished, flat surfaces to suppress topographic and geometric effects; polishing must not be followed by chemical or electrochemical etching because it can alter the interrogated near-surface composition. For low-energy characteristic X-rays below 1 keV, surface scratches should be reduced below approximately 50 nm rms. Unknowns and standards should have comparable coating thickness, since differences can cause significant errors, particularly at beam energies below about 5 keV. Standards may be co-mounted or placed on a separate mount, and can include pure elements, stoichiometric compounds, alloys, glasses, or minerals, but multiphase standards must have accurately known compositions and micrometer-scale homogeneity. Unknowns and standards must be measured using identical, reproducible beam energy, dose, detector geometry, specimen tilt, and EDS settings; approximately 10% detector deadtime is recommended to limit coincidence peaks. Under these controls, Table 5 reports relative errors of roughly 0–3.6% for sulfide analyses, and the authors state that performance falls within established EPMA/WDS error limits. The excerpt does not specify bulk-dimension requirements, so that condition cannot be assessed here.

## pqac-00000024

From text 'newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Performing elemental microanalysis with high accuracy and high precision by scanning electron microscopy/silicon drift detector energy-dispersive x-ray spectrometry (sem/sdd-eds). Journal of Materials Science, 50:493-518, Nov 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2, doi:10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2. This article has 630 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt states that high-accuracy SEM/SDD-EDS k-ratio analysis requires careful measurement practice, including appropriate surface preparation of both unknowns and standards. These surfaces must be polished so that relief is no greater than 50 nm rms, and the specimen must approximate an ideal flat surface positioned at known angles relative to the electron beam and spectrometer. Local surface inclination and specimen thickness otherwise introduce strong geometric effects. The excerpt does not explicitly specify bulk dimensions, homogeneity, or a requirement that standards and specimens be measured under identical conditions, although the emphasis on controlled geometry and matrix-correction conditions implies that departures from the reference setup are consequential. Under suitable conditions, the article reports routine accuracy within ±5% relative for major constituents (mass fraction above 0.1), ±10% for minor constituents (0.01–0.1), and ±25% for trace constituents (0.001–0.01); detection limits as low as 0.0005 mass fraction may be achieved. For rough or otherwise non-ideal specimens, errors can exceed those of the ideal flat-specimen case by orders of magnitude. Normalization to 100% can conceal these problems, whereas the k-ratio protocol and analytical total provide an important warning. In such cases, reported concentrations may be unreliable or of dubious value.

## pqac-00000025

From text 'newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 6-7'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Journal of Materials Science, 50:493-518, Nov 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2, doi:10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2. This article has 630 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt shows that high-accuracy SEM/SDD-EDS k-ratio analysis depends on maintaining an ideal, standards-compatible specimen geometry: a flat, highly polished bulk surface, with a thin (<10 nm) conductive carbon coating when needed for charge dissipation. The K411 glass results used a 0.1 µm alumina final polish, 20 randomly selected analyses, 20 keV excitation, and standards including pure Mg, Si, and Fe, with Ca supplied by a certified glass standard; oxygen was calculated from assumed cation stoichiometry. Under these conditions, the average elemental results agreed closely with the SRM certificate, with relative errors from -1.1% to +1.8%. Homogeneity is assessed through the tight clustering of repeated analyses, while an apparent outlier was traced to a residual scratch rather than composition. Violating flatness and polish—even with a surface that did not look especially rough in an SEM—caused systematic concentration shifts and greater scatter. More severe departures, including 600-grit scratches, fracture surfaces, holes, chips, shards, and other irregular geometries, produced apparent Mg and Fe concentrations spanning nearly an order of magnitude, making the results dubious for many applications. This excerpt does not explicitly state bulk-dimension or identical-condition requirements beyond the need for suitable standards and comparable ideal geometry.

## pqac-00000026

From text 'newbury2013quantitativesemedsstep pages 1-2'.

D.E. Newbury and N.W. Ritchie. Quantitative sem/eds, step 1: what constitutes a sufficiently flat specimen? Microscopy and Microanalysis, 19:1244-1245, Aug 2013. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927613008210, doi:10.1017/s1431927613008210. This article has 20 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt states that high-accuracy SEM/EDS k-ratio analysis requires the unknown and standards to be prepared and measured so that differences in measured x-ray intensities arise only from composition. This implicitly requires comparable measurement conditions and specimen geometry, especially a sufficiently flat, highly polished surface; otherwise roughness changes x-ray generation and escape differently in the unknown and standard. Surface relief is particularly damaging for low-energy characteristic x-rays such as O K (0.523 keV) and Fe L (0.704 keV). Monte Carlo simulations for a crenellated FeO surface found relative effects of at least 5% even for grooves approximately 100 nm high and laterally spaced, while reducing relief below 20 nm lowered the roughness contribution below 1% for these photons. Severe geometric effects can produce relative errors as large as a factor of 10. The passage notes use of pure gold and homogeneous brass in an earlier roughness study, but it does not provide explicit requirements for bulk dimensions, specimen thickness, or compositional homogeneity beyond these examples. It also does not quantify accuracy losses from violating bulk or homogeneity conditions, nor does it give a general achieved accuracy value; it only indicates that k-ratio SEM/EDS can match EPMA/WDS precision and accuracy under appropriate conditions.

The excerpt indicates that high-accuracy, standards-based SEM-EDS k-ratio analysis depends on matching the measurement conditions for standards and unknown specimens and on maintaining controlled specimen geometry. The specimen should approximate an ideal flat surface, positioned at known angles relative to the electron beam and X-ray spectrometer; departures from this geometry can produce very large changes in measured X-ray intensities, particularly when low- and high-energy lines are analyzed together. Differences between standards and unknowns in coating thickness or native surface-oxide thickness are specifically identified as uncontrolled experimental deviations that can distort results. The excerpt does not explicitly enumerate requirements for polish, bulk dimensions, or homogeneity, although these are consistent with the stated need for controlled geometry and comparable conditions. Under a standards-based protocol, an example Cu-Au alloy analysis at 20 keV produced relative errors generally around 0–1.6%, with analytical totals of 0.988–1.007; totals near 0.98–1.02 are presented as normal consequences of measurement and correction uncertainties. By contrast, standardless analysis, which lacks the same absolute standard/experimental control, can have an error range of approximately ±30% for 95% of results, and some sulfide analyses exceed 20% error. From text 'newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. The excerpt emphasizes that high-accuracy SEM/EDS quantification requires controlling specimen geometry rather than relying on automatic normalization. The example of NIST SRM 470 uses a microscopically homogeneous glass prepared as a flat, highly polished bulk specimen, with a final 100 nm alumina polish and a thin (<10 nm) carbon coating for charge dissipation. These conditions provide an ideal geometry for standards-based k-ratio analysis. Shape, specimen size, surface damage, voids, chips, shards, and local surface inclination alter electron scattering and the X-ray path length to the detector, thereby changing absorption and measured intensities. Consequently, specimens and standards need comparable, controlled geometry and surface condition for accurate k-ratio results; the excerpt specifically documents the ideal specimen preparation but does not state a numerical accuracy limit or explicitly detail all matching requirements. Violating these conditions can produce large, uncontrolled, and potentially unrecognized errors. Internal normalization to unity conceals the resulting analytical-total deviations, creating an appearance of accuracy while removing an important diagnostic of geometry-related error. The figures compare ideal bulk material with scratched, holed, chipped, and shard forms, illustrating that accuracy is substantially compromised when flatness, polish, bulk form, and geometry are not maintained.

Quantification then depends on matrix corrections for electron scattering and energy loss, X-ray absorption, and secondary fluorescence. The excerpt does not specify explicit flatness, polish, or bulk-dimension requirements, although its discussion of near-surface sampling implies that the analyzed surface must represent the material; altered or unrepresentative near-surface composition compromises the result. A mature WDS k-ratio/matrix-correction procedure achieved a relative-error standard deviation of about 2.5% for major constituents. function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a concise technical table summarizing artifact, mechanism, expected EDS/EPMA bias, and mitigation for epoxy-mounted pure-metal particles used as quantification standards. Include finite particle/edge effects, native oxide shells at particle-epoxy boundaries, pores/pull-out/epoxy intrusion, polishing relief and scratches, smearing/plastic flow of soft tin, contamination/embedded abrasive, electrical grounding/coating, and secondary fluorescence. Make clear bulk polished standards avoid or reduce these issues."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Artifact | Mechanism in an epoxy-mounted metal particle | Expected EDS/EPMA bias | Mitigation; comparison with bulk standard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Finite particle / edge effects | If the beam is too close to the particle–epoxy boundary, electrons and generated X-rays escape the metal, while backscattered electrons may excite the epoxy or neighboring material. Local edge slope also changes take-off angle and absorption path. | Reduced metal intensity, low analytical totals, apparent C/O or neighboring-element signal, and line-dependent errors—usually greatest for low-energy X-rays. Normalizing to 100% can hide the problem. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000024) | Use grains many times larger than the full interaction region; analyze only the broad, flat center, at least several interaction-volume radii from every visible boundary. Confirm by line scans or measurements at increasing edge distance. A large bulk polished standard effectively eliminates finite-size edges. |
| Native oxide shell at particle–epoxy boundary | Powder’s original external oxide becomes an internal rim around the polished metal cross-section; polishing may also form a new oxide film on the exposed face. Small grains have high oxide-to-metal volume and boundary ratios. | O signal and depressed apparent metal concentration if the interaction volume intersects the rim; beam-energy-dependent results; low-energy metal lines may be attenuated. Different oxide thicknesses on standard and unknown invalidate ideal k-ratio cancellation. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027) | Select coarse, freshly cleaned granules; measure well inside the metallic core; repolish immediately before use and store dry/inert where warranted. Map O and reject rim-affected grains. Bulk metal has far less boundary oxide per usable area, although its exposed face can still oxidize. |
| Pores, pull-out, and epoxy intrusion | Poor wetting, trapped air, particle packing, or grinding pull-out leaves voids and resin-filled fissures beside or beneath the apparent metal surface. | Loss of metal X-ray yield, C/O contribution, charging, abnormal continuum, low totals, and irreproducible results as the beam overlaps hidden resin or voids. Geometry and specimen-size defects can cause large concentration shifts. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) | Vacuum-impregnate with low-viscosity epoxy, disperse particles rather than allowing contact, grind deeply enough to expose sound interiors, and reject grains showing pores in BSE imaging. Dense bulk standards largely avoid resin intrusion and pull-out. |
| Polishing relief, scratches, or rounded edges | Large hardness contrast between metal and epoxy produces differential wear; abrasive polishing may round particle margins, plough grooves, or leave scratches comparable to the X-ray generation depth. | Changed electron scattering and X-ray escape paths; strongly absorbed low-energy lines may vary by several percent to orders of magnitude. Even residual scratches can create outlying analyses. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | Use rigid, low-nap cloths, light loads, progressively fine abrasives, and a suitable final polish; verify flatness by SE/BSE imaging and avoid all relief and scratches. Bulk pieces are easier to polish coplanar and provide much larger relief-free areas. |
| Smearing / plastic flow of soft Sn | Tin deforms and ploughs rather than cutting cleanly; polishing can drag Sn across epoxy, pores, oxide rims, or adjacent standards and can fold altered surface material over the exposed core. | Locally elevated Sn outside the grain; variable Sn/O/C within it; concealed pores or oxide; an unrepresentative mechanically worked surface and poor repeatability. Micro-ploughing and wear-debris transfer are recognized preparation artifacts. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000015) | Use minimal force and heat, sharp fine abrasives, short polishing times, rigid support, and a validated Sn-specific metallographic procedure; clean between stages and inspect maps for Sn tails. A larger bulk Sn coupon is better supported but remains susceptible to smearing. |
| Contamination or embedded abrasive | Diamond, alumina, colloidal silica, lubricant, wear debris, or metal transferred from neighboring standards can lodge in scratches, pores, or the soft metal surface. | Spurious C, O, Al, Si, or neighboring-metal peaks; diluted metal concentration; heterogeneous spot results. Polishing discs contaminated by wear debris can transfer reaction products or material between phases. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014) | Use dedicated clean consumables, thorough ultrasonic or solvent cleaning where chemically safe, and separate polishing of easily cross-contaminating metals. Screen by maps and reject inclusions. Bulk standards reduce boundary trapping but still require contamination control. |
| Poor electrical grounding / unequal coating | Isolated metal grains may not contact the conductive mount because epoxy surrounds them; charging changes landing energy and beam position. A carbon or metal coating also absorbs X-rays if its thickness differs between standard and unknown. | Count-rate instability, peak shifts, beam drift, altered effective overvoltage, and systematic low-energy-line errors; unequal coating thickness prevents cancellation in the k-ratio. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000027) | Provide a conductive path with carbon paint or a metal-filled mounting route where appropriate; coat standard and unknown together or to matched, monitored thickness. Bulk metal is readily grounded and often needs no coating. |
| Secondary fluorescence / remote excitation | Characteristic or continuum X-rays and backscattered electrons can excite adjacent particles, mounting hardware, or epoxy additives outside the primary electron interaction volume; the fluorescence range can reach tens of micrometres. | False trace/minor peaks or elevated intensities from nearby materials even when the primary interaction volume remains inside the target grain. Bulk-specimen guidance gives typical secondary-fluorescence dimensions of roughly 10–100 µm. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000019) | Space grains and unlike standards widely, avoid metal-filled epoxy unless modeled, analyze central regions, and check suspect elements against blank epoxy and isolated grains. A large isolated bulk standard minimizes neighboring-material fluorescence but does not eliminate chamber or holder contributions. |


*Table: Preparation and geometry artifacts that can bias quantitative SEM-EDS or EPMA of epoxy-mounted pure-metal particles, with practical controls and the advantages of bulk polished standards.*

function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Epoxy-mounted metal powders as SEM-EDS/EPMA standards

## Conclusion

**Yes—with qualifications.** Embedding high-purity metal grains or fragments in epoxy and polishing through them is an established and technically valid way to make a **working SEM-EDS or EPMA standard mount**. The epoxy itself is not disqualifying if the exposed metallic cross-section is flat, homogeneous, electrically grounded, and sufficiently large that the analyzed point behaves as a semi-infinite bulk specimen. Standards may be co-mounted or kept on a separate mount, and pure elements are acceptable k-ratio standards when their composition and surface condition are known. However, standards practice favors large, independently characterized fragments—approximately millimetre-sized material rather than 10-µm grains—and a mounted powder should not automatically be treated as metrologically equivalent to a certified bulk polished coupon. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029)

For high-accuracy work, both standard and unknown must be highly polished and unetched, homogeneous on the micrometre scale, and measured at the same beam energy, dose, incidence/take-off geometry, detector conditions, and preferably matched coating thickness. Under such controls, standards-based SEM-EDS can produce approximately 1–3% relative errors in favorable major-element cases and routinely target ±5% for major constituents; nonideal geometry can instead produce errors from tens of percent to nearly an order of magnitude. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027)

## Required particle size

There is **no universal minimum diameter**. It depends on beam energy, atomic number, density, X-ray line, detector geometry, and whether secondary fluorescence matters. The Kanaya–Okayama electron-range estimate is

\[
R_{KO}(\mu\mathrm{m})=\frac{0.0276\,A\,E_0^{1.67}}{Z^{0.89}\rho},
\]

where \(A\) is atomic mass, \(Z\) atomic number, \(\rho\) density in g cm⁻³, and \(E_0\) beam energy in keV. It estimates maximum electron penetration, not the exact X-ray generation diameter. (pqac-00000016)

Representative Kanaya–Okayama ranges calculated from that equation are:

| Metal | 15 kV | 20 kV |
|---|---:|---:|
| Al | ~2.9 µm | ~4.7 µm |
| Fe | ~1.1 µm | ~1.7 µm |
| Cu | ~1.0 µm | ~1.6 µm |
| Sn | ~1.4 µm | ~2.2 µm |
| Au | ~0.8 µm | ~1.3 µm |

These are approximate maximum-depth scales; the lateral and useful X-ray generation dimensions must be checked by Monte Carlo simulation for the actual material and lines. Published microanalysis guidance places the 20-keV interaction scale broadly around 1–5 µm and notes that primary X-ray production in bulk SEM-EDS commonly spans approximately 0.5–10 µm. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019)

A conservative practical criterion is therefore:

* use a polished metallic cross-section **at least 5–10 times the largest primary interaction dimension**;
* place the beam **at least 2–3 interaction-volume radii from every metal–epoxy boundary, pore, oxide rim, or neighboring particle**;
* at 15–20 kV, prefer exposed sections **≥20–50 µm across** for routine major-element standardization; larger is better, and approximately 1-mm fragments are preferable where available;
* regard **~10-µm particles as marginal, especially at 20 kV**, for low-density metals such as Al, for points not exactly centered, or where polishing has left only a shallow cap;
* verify adequacy experimentally by moving the beam toward the edge and by comparing 15- and 20-kV results. A stable central plateau is required.

The 5–10× rule is a conservative engineering recommendation rather than a formal universal standard. It is consistent with experiments that used 20–200 µm particles explicitly larger than the interaction volume and found that an ~80-µm particle was effectively flat only near its top center. Conventional matrix corrections did not remove errors caused by curvature, edge position, or altered absorption paths. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005)

A second, longer length scale applies to **secondary X-ray fluorescence**, which can extend roughly 10–100 µm. Consequently, a 20–50 µm grain may be adequate for major-element k-ratios yet still be imperfect for trace analysis if adjacent particles, metal-filled resin, the mount, or oxide-rich boundaries contain interfering elements. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000019)

## Accuracy-limiting artifacts

The main limitations and controls are summarized below.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Surface oxide films

Powders have much more original surface area than bulk coupons. Their native oxide becomes a circumferential internal rim when the grain is sectioned, while polishing and subsequent air exposure can create a new altered film on the exposed face. Polishing-induced metal oxides can range from a few nanometres to hundreds of nanometres. If the interaction volume intersects an oxide rim, the result contains O, gives depressed metal intensity, and no longer represents the nominal pure metal. Differences in native-oxide thickness between standard and unknown also defeat ideal k-ratio cancellation. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027)

A nanometre-scale oxide on the central face may have little effect at 15–20 kV for hard metal K lines, but it can matter for oxygen measurement and low-energy metal L/M lines. A micrometre-scale oxidized particle boundary is unacceptable if sampled. Use coarse freshly cleaned granules, map O, analyze only the metallic core, repolish shortly before use, and store oxidation-sensitive standards dry or inert.

### Porosity, pull-out, and epoxy intrusion

Entrapped air, inadequate resin infiltration, agglomerated powder, or grinding pull-out can leave resin-filled pores or subsurface voids. These reduce metal X-ray production, add C/O, alter the continuum, cause charging, and can produce low totals even when the surface appears metallic. Shape, holes, chips, shards, and voids are documented causes of large and scattered SEM-EDS errors. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028)

Vacuum impregnation with low-viscosity epoxy, widely separated grains, sufficiently deep sectioning, and BSE inspection are necessary. Reject any particle whose central analytical region contains pores, cracks, resin tongues, or pull-out.

### Relief, scratches, and particle edges

The metal–epoxy hardness contrast promotes differential polishing relief and rounded margins. Local slope changes electron backscattering, detector take-off angle, and X-ray absorption path. Effects are strongest for soft X-rays: rough Cu–Au surfaces produced Cu-L/Cu-K errors from −92% to +42%, and even ~100-nm relief can affect O-K and Fe-L intensities by at least 5%. Relief below approximately 20 nm reduced the modeled contribution below 1%; rigorous practical guidance calls for roughly 50-nm-rms or better surfaces for low-energy analysis. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026)

Near a particle edge, electrons can leave the metal and excite epoxy or nearby phases, and X-rays may experience abnormal escape or absorption paths. Remote excitation by backscattered electrons may also generate apparently real minor or trace peaks outside the intended interaction region. Conventional ZAF or φ(ρz) corrections assume flat bulk geometry and do not correct these effects automatically. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006)

| Al | ~2.9 µm | ~4.7 µm |
| Fe | ~1.1 µm | ~1.7 µm |
| Cu | ~1.0 µm | ~1.6 µm |
| Sn | ~1.4 µm | ~2.2 µm |
| Au | ~0.8 µm | ~1.3 µm |

Near a particle edge, electrons can leave the metal and excite epoxy or nearby phases, and X-rays may experience abnormal escape or absorption paths. Remote excitation by backscattered electrons may also generate apparently real minor or trace peaks outside the intended interaction region. Conventional ZAF or φ(ρz) corrections assume flat bulk geometry and do not correct these effects automatically. (newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 1-2, newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 11-12, newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 6-8)

### Smearing of soft metals, especially tin

Sn is mechanically soft and prone to plastic flow. Under excessive load or a compliant cloth it can plough and smear rather than cut cleanly, dragging Sn across epoxy, oxide rims, pores, or adjacent standards and folding altered material over the metallic core. The general polishing literature documents micro-ploughing, wear-debris transfer, and disproportionate deformation of soft phases; these mechanisms directly explain the familiar Sn-preparation problem, although the cited evidence does not establish a universal numerical Sn error. (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 21-22, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 3-4)

Use rigid low-nap support, low force and heat, fresh sharp fine abrasive, short polishing steps, thorough cleaning between stages, and an Sn-validated metallographic procedure. Inspect Sn and O maps for tails or films outside the nominal grain. A bulk Sn coupon is better supported and offers a larger clean area, but it too can smear.

## Recommended acceptance test

An epoxy-mounted granular standard should be accepted only after it passes the following checks:

1. **Pedigree:** documented purity and impurity inventory, preferably independently characterized rather than assigned solely by EDS/EPMA. High nominal purity does not establish homogeneity or absence of oxide. (carpenter2008epmastandardsthe pages 1-2, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2)
2. **Geometry:** a flat, unetched central area ≥5–10 interaction dimensions across, with no edge, pore, crack, or second phase within at least 2–3 interaction radii.
3. **Preparation:** minimal relief and scratches; matched conductive coating and reliable grounding. Standards and unknowns should be prepared and measured comparably. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 2-4, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 11-13)
4. **Imaging/maps:** BSE plus O, C, and target-metal maps to identify oxide rims, epoxy intrusion, polishing debris, and smearing.
5. **Repeatability:** multiple central points on several particles should agree within counting statistics and the laboratory’s control limits. Do not normalize away poor analytical totals; totals are a diagnostic for geometry and contamination. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6)
6. **Voltage/edge test:** compare central results at 15 and 20 kV and acquire an edge-distance profile. Systematic voltage dependence or drift toward the edge indicates finite size, oxide, porosity, or layered-surface effects.
7. **Traceability:** compare the mounted-particle standard against a validated bulk polished standard. If major-element ratios differ by more than the intended uncertainty—typically a few percent for rigorous standards-based work—the granular mount should be treated only as qualitative or semiquantitative. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 2-4, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 4-5)

Thus, **coarse epoxy-mounted granules are accepted as practical working standards when validated**, but fine powders are a compromise. For the most accurate EPMA/SEM-EDS calibration—particularly low-energy lines, oxygen, trace constituents, or interlaboratory work—large, dense, polished bulk standards remain preferable because they provide much more edge-free area and reduce oxide-boundary, porosity, resin, relief, grounding, and secondary-fluorescence artifacts.
