# Epoxy-mounted metal powders as SEM-EDS/EPMA standards

## Conclusion

**Yes—with qualifications.** Embedding high-purity metal grains or fragments in epoxy and polishing through them is an established and technically valid way to make a **working SEM-EDS or EPMA standard mount**. The epoxy itself is not disqualifying if the exposed metallic cross-section is flat, homogeneous, electrically grounded, and sufficiently large that the analyzed point behaves as a semi-infinite bulk specimen. Standards may be co-mounted or kept on a separate mount, and pure elements are acceptable k-ratio standards when their composition and surface condition are known. However, standards practice favors large, independently characterized fragments—approximately millimetre-sized material rather than 10-µm grains—and a mounted powder should not automatically be treated as metrologically equivalent to a certified bulk polished coupon. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029)

For high-accuracy work, both standard and unknown must be highly polished and unetched, homogeneous on the micrometre scale, and measured at the same beam energy, dose, incidence/take-off geometry, detector conditions, and preferably matched coating thickness. Under such controls, standards-based SEM-EDS can produce approximately 1–3% relative errors in favorable major-element cases and routinely target ±5% for major constituents; nonideal geometry can instead produce errors from tens of percent to nearly an order of magnitude. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027)

## Required particle size

There is **no universal minimum diameter**. It depends on beam energy, atomic number, density, X-ray line, detector geometry, and whether secondary fluorescence matters. The Kanaya–Okayama electron-range estimate is

\[
R_{KO}(\mu\mathrm{m})=\frac{0.0276\,A\,E_0^{1.67}}{Z^{0.89}\rho},
\]

where \(A\) is atomic mass, \(Z\) atomic number, \(\rho\) density in g cm⁻³, and \(E_0\) beam energy in keV. It estimates maximum electron penetration, not the exact X-ray generation diameter. (pqac-00000016)

Representative Kanaya–Okayama ranges calculated from that equation are:

| Metal | 15 kV | 20 kV |
|---|---:|---:|
| Al | ~2.9 µm | ~4.7 µm |
| Fe | ~1.1 µm | ~1.7 µm |
| Cu | ~1.0 µm | ~1.6 µm |
| Sn | ~1.4 µm | ~2.2 µm |
| Au | ~0.8 µm | ~1.3 µm |

These are approximate maximum-depth scales; the lateral and useful X-ray generation dimensions must be checked by Monte Carlo simulation for the actual material and lines. Published microanalysis guidance places the 20-keV interaction scale broadly around 1–5 µm and notes that primary X-ray production in bulk SEM-EDS commonly spans approximately 0.5–10 µm. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019)

A conservative practical criterion is therefore:

* use a polished metallic cross-section **at least 5–10 times the largest primary interaction dimension**;
* place the beam **at least 2–3 interaction-volume radii from every metal–epoxy boundary, pore, oxide rim, or neighboring particle**;
* at 15–20 kV, prefer exposed sections **≥20–50 µm across** for routine major-element standardization; larger is better, and approximately 1-mm fragments are preferable where available;
* regard **~10-µm particles as marginal, especially at 20 kV**, for low-density metals such as Al, for points not exactly centered, or where polishing has left only a shallow cap;
* verify adequacy experimentally by moving the beam toward the edge and by comparing 15- and 20-kV results. A stable central plateau is required.

The 5–10× rule is a conservative engineering recommendation rather than a formal universal standard. It is consistent with experiments that used 20–200 µm particles explicitly larger than the interaction volume and found that an ~80-µm particle was effectively flat only near its top center. Conventional matrix corrections did not remove errors caused by curvature, edge position, or altered absorption paths. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005)

A second, longer length scale applies to **secondary X-ray fluorescence**, which can extend roughly 10–100 µm. Consequently, a 20–50 µm grain may be adequate for major-element k-ratios yet still be imperfect for trace analysis if adjacent particles, metal-filled resin, the mount, or oxide-rich boundaries contain interfering elements. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000019)

## Accuracy-limiting artifacts

The main limitations and controls are summarized below.

| Artifact | Mechanism in an epoxy-mounted metal particle | Expected EDS/EPMA bias | Mitigation; comparison with bulk standard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Finite particle / edge effects | If the beam is too close to the particle–epoxy boundary, electrons and generated X-rays escape the metal, while backscattered electrons may excite the epoxy or neighboring material. Local edge slope also changes take-off angle and absorption path. | Reduced metal intensity, low analytical totals, apparent C/O or neighboring-element signal, and line-dependent errors—usually greatest for low-energy X-rays. Normalizing to 100% can hide the problem. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000024) | Use grains many times larger than the full interaction region; analyze only the broad, flat center, at least several interaction-volume radii from every visible boundary. Confirm by line scans or measurements at increasing edge distance. A large bulk polished standard effectively eliminates finite-size edges. |
| Native oxide shell at particle–epoxy boundary | Powder’s original external oxide becomes an internal rim around the polished metal cross-section; polishing may also form a new oxide film on the exposed face. Small grains have high oxide-to-metal volume and boundary ratios. | O signal and depressed apparent metal concentration if the interaction volume intersects the rim; beam-energy-dependent results; low-energy metal lines may be attenuated. Different oxide thicknesses on standard and unknown invalidate ideal k-ratio cancellation. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027) | Select coarse, freshly cleaned granules; measure well inside the metallic core; repolish immediately before use and store dry/inert where warranted. Map O and reject rim-affected grains. Bulk metal has far less boundary oxide per usable area, although its exposed face can still oxidize. |
| Pores, pull-out, and epoxy intrusion | Poor wetting, trapped air, particle packing, or grinding pull-out leaves voids and resin-filled fissures beside or beneath the apparent metal surface. | Loss of metal X-ray yield, C/O contribution, charging, abnormal continuum, low totals, and irreproducible results as the beam overlaps hidden resin or voids. Geometry and specimen-size defects can cause large concentration shifts. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) | Vacuum-impregnate with low-viscosity epoxy, disperse particles rather than allowing contact, grind deeply enough to expose sound interiors, and reject grains showing pores in BSE imaging. Dense bulk standards largely avoid resin intrusion and pull-out. |
| Polishing relief, scratches, or rounded edges | Large hardness contrast between metal and epoxy produces differential wear; abrasive polishing may round particle margins, plough grooves, or leave scratches comparable to the X-ray generation depth. | Changed electron scattering and X-ray escape paths; strongly absorbed low-energy lines may vary by several percent to orders of magnitude. Even residual scratches can create outlying analyses. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | Use rigid, low-nap cloths, light loads, progressively fine abrasives, and a suitable final polish; verify flatness by SE/BSE imaging and avoid all relief and scratches. Bulk pieces are easier to polish coplanar and provide much larger relief-free areas. |
| Smearing / plastic flow of soft Sn | Tin deforms and ploughs rather than cutting cleanly; polishing can drag Sn across epoxy, pores, oxide rims, or adjacent standards and can fold altered surface material over the exposed core. | Locally elevated Sn outside the grain; variable Sn/O/C within it; concealed pores or oxide; an unrepresentative mechanically worked surface and poor repeatability. Micro-ploughing and wear-debris transfer are recognized preparation artifacts. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000015) | Use minimal force and heat, sharp fine abrasives, short polishing times, rigid support, and a validated Sn-specific metallographic procedure; clean between stages and inspect maps for Sn tails. A larger bulk Sn coupon is better supported but remains susceptible to smearing. |
| Contamination or embedded abrasive | Diamond, alumina, colloidal silica, lubricant, wear debris, or metal transferred from neighboring standards can lodge in scratches, pores, or the soft metal surface. | Spurious C, O, Al, Si, or neighboring-metal peaks; diluted metal concentration; heterogeneous spot results. Polishing discs contaminated by wear debris can transfer reaction products or material between phases. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014) | Use dedicated clean consumables, thorough ultrasonic or solvent cleaning where chemically safe, and separate polishing of easily cross-contaminating metals. Screen by maps and reject inclusions. Bulk standards reduce boundary trapping but still require contamination control. |
| Poor electrical grounding / unequal coating | Isolated metal grains may not contact the conductive mount because epoxy surrounds them; charging changes landing energy and beam position. A carbon or metal coating also absorbs X-rays if its thickness differs between standard and unknown. | Count-rate instability, peak shifts, beam drift, altered effective overvoltage, and systematic low-energy-line errors; unequal coating thickness prevents cancellation in the k-ratio. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000027) | Provide a conductive path with carbon paint or a metal-filled mounting route where appropriate; coat standard and unknown together or to matched, monitored thickness. Bulk metal is readily grounded and often needs no coating. |
| Secondary fluorescence / remote excitation | Characteristic or continuum X-rays and backscattered electrons can excite adjacent particles, mounting hardware, or epoxy additives outside the primary electron interaction volume; the fluorescence range can reach tens of micrometres. | False trace/minor peaks or elevated intensities from nearby materials even when the primary interaction volume remains inside the target grain. Bulk-specimen guidance gives typical secondary-fluorescence dimensions of roughly 10–100 µm. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000019) | Space grains and unlike standards widely, avoid metal-filled epoxy unless modeled, analyze central regions, and check suspect elements against blank epoxy and isolated grains. A large isolated bulk standard minimizes neighboring-material fluorescence but does not eliminate chamber or holder contributions. |


*Table: Preparation and geometry artifacts that can bias quantitative SEM-EDS or EPMA of epoxy-mounted pure-metal particles, with practical controls and the advantages of bulk polished standards.*

### Surface oxide films

Powders have much more original surface area than bulk coupons. Their native oxide becomes a circumferential internal rim when the grain is sectioned, while polishing and subsequent air exposure can create a new altered film on the exposed face. Polishing-induced metal oxides can range from a few nanometres to hundreds of nanometres. If the interaction volume intersects an oxide rim, the result contains O, gives depressed metal intensity, and no longer represents the nominal pure metal. Differences in native-oxide thickness between standard and unknown also defeat ideal k-ratio cancellation. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027)

A micrometre-scale oxidized particle boundary is unacceptable if sampled. Use coarse freshly cleaned granules, map O, analyze only the metallic core, repolish shortly before use, and store oxidation-sensitive standards dry or inert.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that quantitative EPMA/SEM-EDS is strongly dependent on specimen geometry, detector visibility, and the relationship between the electron beam, analyzed surface, and EDS takeoff path. It does not specifically provide particle-size criteria, interaction-volume dimensions, or a direct comparison between polished bulk standards and particles embedded in epoxy. For polished, flat bulk standards, the geometry is comparatively controlled, but detector and instrument configuration can still introduce backscatter and rescattering effects. For rough, tilted, recessed, or particle-like specimens, surrounding topography can block characteristic x-rays, increase absorption, and produce remote excitation: backscattered electrons may strike adjacent regions and generate nonlocalized x-rays that appear as trace, minor, or major constituents. The recommended mitigation is careful reorientation, preferably with the beam normal to the surface and the feature on the detector-facing side; however, low-angle or recessed regions can still contribute spurious signal. The passage therefore supports treating embedded particles as geometrically non-ideal targets and warns that standards must reproduce relevant excitation and detection geometry where possible. It does not establish a numerical requirement that particles exceed the interaction volume, nor does it quantify edge effects specifically at 15–20 keV. It does describe peak-to-local-background ratios as an internal monitor for geometry-related changes.

The quantitative model and mass-absorption treatment are initially formulated for a flat, bulk sample, and the empirical parameters are calibrated using bulk, polished standards. contexts.context: This excerpt establishes that quantitative EPMA/SEM-EDS measurements on polished bulk standards are sensitive to the final surface-preparation procedure and to charging caused by polishing-induced surface or subsurface damage. In ZnS, colloidal-silica polishing did not eliminate charging defects: the Duane–Hunt limit shifted with irradiation time, continuous x-ray emission could not always be modeled using a single constant landing energy, and dielectric breakdown or beam displacement could produce rapid intensity changes. Thus, a polished flat bulk standard must have a sufficiently damage-free, electrically stable surface, and its charging state must be controlled or monitored during quantitative analysis. The alumina comparison further shows that mechanically diamond-polished and silica-polished surfaces can produce different Al and O intensities, especially at low incident energy (5 keV); the ratios move closer to unity as analyzed depth increases (15–25 keV), indicating reduced sensitivity to near-surface preparation effects. The excerpt compares single-crystal, polycrystalline, and massive specimens, but it does not directly establish requirements for particles embedded in epoxy, particle dimensions relative to the electron interaction volume, or specific edge/geometry effects at 15–20 keV. Those conclusions would require additional literature addressing finite particles, substrate contributions, and lateral/edge fluorescence or beam spreading.

It also emphasizes that SEM images can make highly irregular specimens appear readily examinable even when their geometry is unsuitable for quantitative x-ray analysis. Surface relief changes both the primary-electron interaction and the x-ray absorption path length, so measured intensities can be substantially modified by geometry; these effects are particularly strong for low-energy lines, although absorption changes occur at all photon energies. contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that polished cross sections or flat bulk surfaces provide the reference analyses for quantitative EPMA, using conventional ZAF matrix corrections and pure-element standards. For particles, geometry must be considered in relation to the electron interaction volume: an approximately 80 µm spherical particle is treated as effectively flat at its top center when its curvature is much larger than the interaction volume. At other positions, particle curvature changes the x-ray take-off angle and absorption path. At 20 keV, moving toward the EDS raises the low-energy (<4 keV) intensity because the take-off angle increases and absorption decreases, whereas moving away from the EDS produces strong low-energy attenuation as x-rays traverse more particle material. The high-energy (>4 keV) portion is comparatively insensitive to these added paths. Conventional ZAF results therefore can show geometry-driven errors, especially for low-energy lines: a backside position produced an anomalously low analytical total (Σ = 0.834), while a toward-EDS position gave Σ = 1.037. Normalized concentrations may substantially misrepresent low-energy elements when they are absorbed. The excerpt does not specifically establish epoxy-mounting requirements or a universal particle-size threshold; it supports comparing embedded-particle results with polished-section standards and ensuring particle dimensions/curvature exceed the interaction-volume scale where a flat-surface approximation is intended.

contexts.context: The excerpt specifically documents roughness and topographic artifacts produced by abrading a polished metal standard. Surface geometry changes both the primary-electron interaction and the X-ray absorption path length, causing substantial intensity variations even when the bulk composition is homogeneous. These effects are strongest for low-energy lines, such as Cu-Lα and Au-Mα, although roughness-related absorption changes affect photons at all energies. High-energy Cu-Kα is comparatively insensitive, with an expected variation of about 2% for micrometer-scale features, and can function as an internal reference for evaluating low-energy distortions. Point analyses on the rough Cu–Au alloy produced Cu-L/Cu-K relative errors ranging from −92% to +42%, far exceeding ordinary counting and deconvolution uncertainty. Scanning larger areas reduces random variation but does not necessarily remove systematic bias: the largest scan showed Cu-L intensity approximately 20% below the ideal and Cu-K approximately 6% below it. The excerpt does not provide evidence about polishing-induced chemical contamination, deformation, edge rounding, porosity, relief, or smearing; its demonstrated concern is geometric roughness/topography and the resulting absorption and excitation artifacts in quantitative X-ray analysis of metals.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies polishing as a major source of artifacts that can compromise quantitative EPMA/X-ray microanalysis. Abrasive preparation produces surface and subsurface mechanical changes, including stresses and strains; geometrical changes such as roughness, grooves, and scratches; chemical changes including contaminants and reaction products; and physical or structural changes involving texture, structure, and lattice defects. These modifications affect analytical accuracy because a polished surface must be optically flat to meet the geometrical requirements of quantitative analysis. Polishing involves decreasing abrasive grain sizes through coarse, intermediate, and final stages: coarse abrasives remove initial topographic and chemical defects, while finer abrasives establish the final EPMA surface. The wear process is governed by applied load, motion, duration, abrasive/specimen interactions, and surrounding or interfacial media. Simultaneous normal and tangential forces can create ploughing grooves or scratches and may cause Hertzian fracture. The excerpt specifically supports concerns about topography, contamination or reaction products, deformation, and subsurface damage. It does not yet provide detailed discussion of edge rounding, porosity, relief, or smearing, nor does it distinguish their effects in metals or soft phases; those topics may occur in later sections on surface characterization and implications for quantitative analysis.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several polishing- and preparation-induced artifacts that can compromise quantitative X-ray microanalysis. In chalcopyrite, polishing produces surface contamination by carbon-, oxygen-, and silver-bearing compounds, while abrasive carriers and subsequent polishing can mechanically remove or dissolve pre-existing surface layers. Polishing also modifies iron-oxide and copper-rich layers, changing surface reflectivity and indicating chemical alteration of the analyzed surface. After exposure to air, polished chalcopyrite develops thicker oxidized layers and colored regions, particularly around holes or fissures; these evolving surface films can alter measured composition and signal generation. Chalcopyrite inclusions in a silver sulfide matrix are especially affected: their lower reflectivity is attributed to contamination, and illumination accelerates tarnishing through growth of a silver-bearing compound or Ag2S layer over the inclusion. For ZnS, mechanical polishing with diamond or alumina can create an amorphous or heavily damaged near-surface layer, whereas CMP better preserves crystallographic information. Mechanical polishing and indentation also alter hardness, produce fissures and grain-boundary revelation, and generate lattice disorder and deep subsurface strain fields. Such damaged, chemically altered, contaminated, or strained volumes can yield analyses that do not represent the underlying bulk. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several polishing-induced artifacts that can compromise quantitative X-ray microanalysis. Mechanical polishing of metals can produce rapid surface oxidation, with oxide layers ranging from a few nanometers to hundreds of nanometers; thermal effects, friction, and electrochemical charging during abrasion accelerate these reactions. In sulfide minerals, polishing can cause sulfur volatilization and formation of metal oxides. Contamination may be transferred from neighboring phases: wear debris can smear matrix material over inclusions, while silver-bearing surface compounds can form or evolve after polishing through light, heat, decomposition, and diffusion. Polishing also leaves a structurally damaged subsurface zone, especially in polycrystalline metals, involving strain hardening, crystallographic preferred orientation, and possible grain-boundary de-cohesion. Repeated finer-abrasive steps reduce earlier damage but introduce new damage, so a thin altered layer may remain undetectable optically. The text further notes layered surface contaminants and continuous composition gradients with depth, both of which can bias measured X-ray intensities. Although not all requested artifact categories are discussed in this excerpt, it directly supports chemical alteration, contamination, smearing, and mechanical deformation/damage as important sources of quantitative-analysis error.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several polishing-induced artifacts that can degrade quantitative X-ray microanalysis. Abrasive wear changes surface topography through material removal and roughness, while also altering the physical and chemical properties of both the surface and subsurface relative to the bulk. Polishing can generate localized heat, excitations, defects, dangling bonds, trapped electrons, and reactive species; these effects produce a chemically modified surface whose composition differs from the underlying material. Such altered layers can bias measured elemental concentrations, especially when the analyzed phase is thin, soft, heterogeneous, or mechanically damaged. Abrasive action may proceed by micro-cutting, which removes material as debris, or micro-ploughing, which plastically displaces material without primary removal; the latter can produce smearing, displaced material, and relief-related measurement errors. Wear depends on abrasive size, hardness relative to the specimen, attack angle, and material mechanical behavior. The excerpt emphasizes that heterogeneous specimens and standards containing multiple phases cannot generally be polished optimally for every constituent, so softer phases may experience disproportionate deformation or removal. It does not explicitly discuss edge rounding, porosity, or contamination, but its discussion of debris, altered composition, surface deformation, and subsurface damage is directly relevant to those broader polishing artifacts.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies polishing and preparation-related surface topography—especially scratches, ridges, trenches, and local surface tilt—as a major source of quantitative EPMA error. These features alter both x-ray generation and, particularly, the absorption path length to the detector. Because absorption depends exponentially on path length, even small changes in relief can produce large local intensity variations, with ridges and scratches either increasing or reducing the path. Roughness on the order of 1–5 µm is noted for a ground Cu–Au alloy surface, comparable to the electron interaction volume for a 20 keV beam. Measurements on such surfaces showed very large variations in Cu-L/Cu-K intensity ratios and strong spectral changes at low photon energies below 4 keV, while higher-energy spectra were more stable. The excerpt reports that grinding and polishing must achieve an optical-quality finish, with residual scratch amplitudes below 100 nm, to fully eliminate significant topographic effects. contexts.context: The excerpt does not discuss polishing-induced chemical contamination, deformation, smearing, porosity, or edge-rounding artifacts in detail. It does, however, document topographic and geometric effects relevant to quantitative X-ray microanalysis of rough or nonplanar metal targets. On an 80 µm IN-100 spherical particle, tilted surfaces and differing beam positions produced substantial errors because the X-ray absorption path changes with local geometry. Aluminum showed a +31% error at a position toward the EDS, attributed to anomalous escape of low-energy Al X-rays through the shortened path created by the highly tilted surface. At a position away from the EDS, several concentrations were strongly underestimated, including Al (up to –67%), Mo (–45%), and Ti (–22%), while the analytical total fell to 0.834. The text emphasizes that an apparently acceptable analytical total can conceal large element-specific errors. It recommends mechanically rotating the specimen so the analyzed feature faces the EDS, thereby minimizing absorption, and warns that image scan rotation changes the apparent detector direction without changing the detector’s true chamber orientation. These findings support the importance of controlling relief, surface tilt, shadowing, and local absorption geometry, but they do not provide evidence about polishing chemistry or mechanically induced surface damage.

contexts.context: The excerpt gives the Kanaya–Okayama electron range relation as RKO (µm) = 0.0276 A E0^1.67/(Z ρ^0.89), where A is atomic mass in g/mol, Z is atomic number, ρ is density in g/cm³, and E0 is beam energy in keV. This range estimates electron penetration depth in the specimen. For the hydrous rhyolitic glasses discussed, calculated penetration depths were provided for 15, 20, and 25 keV, but the numerical values from Table 2 are not included in the excerpt. The text states that alkali-ion migration depth is less than electron penetration depth and less than the depth of maximum implanted electron density. Monte Carlo simulations further indicate that increasing accelerating voltage from 15 to 20 keV increases both penetration depth and the depth of the charge center, while also increasing the maximum dimension of the electron-irradiated interaction volume. Thus, specimen or particle dimensions should exceed the relevant penetration/interaction-volume dimensions to avoid electron-beam effects extending through the entire material. However, this excerpt does not state explicit minimum specimen or particle dimensions at 15–20 keV; those would require the missing Table 2 values or calculation using the equation and the specimen composition and density.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the Kanaya–Okayama electron range equation, nor does it give a numerical electron penetration depth or interaction-volume dimension specifically at 15–20 keV. Its quantitative guidance concerns surface geometry rather than particle-size requirements. A NIST DTSA-II Monte Carlo simulation modeled a crenellated FeO surface, using an incident beam energy of 10 keV, and examined low-energy O K (0.523 keV) and Fe L (0.704 keV) x-rays. The simulation found that geometric effects remained at or above 5% relative for surface crenellations having approximately 100 nm height and lateral spacing. To reduce the roughness-induced error below 1% for these low-energy photons, the surface relief had to be less than 20 nm. Conceptually, this supports the need for specimen surfaces to be much flatter than the relevant x-ray-generation and escape geometry, especially for low-energy x-rays, whose intensities are strongly affected by surface topography. However, these values should not be interpreted as a direct minimum specimen or particle dimension at 15–20 keV, because the excerpt neither states a Kanaya–Okayama range calculation nor connects the 10 keV roughness simulation to particle size or electron penetration depth at the requested beam energies.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the Kanaya–Okayama electron-range equation or a numerical evaluation specifically at 15–20 keV. It does, however, give conceptual and dimensional guidance relevant to selecting specimen or particle size. Bulk specimens should be sufficiently large to contain the electron-excited X-ray generation region, stated as typically 0.5–10 μm, and also the larger region associated with secondary X-ray fluorescence, typically 10–100 μm. For conventional SEM/EDS k-ratio/matrix-correction analysis, the material must be compositionally homogeneous throughout the volume contributing primary characteristic X-rays and secondary fluorescence. Thus, particles or specimens smaller than the relevant interaction or fluorescence dimensions may violate the bulk-specimen assumptions and require geometry-specific treatment. The excerpt also emphasizes that surface condition matters: roughness, scratches, pits, implantation, or differential sputtering can alter electron penetration and X-ray absorption paths. These ranges are general values rather than an explicit 15–20 keV calculation; the surrounding chapter’s contents indicate that beam energy is selected as an instrumentation parameter, but the supplied pages do not connect a particular Kanaya–Okayama range to 15 or 20 keV.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not directly address whether EPMA standards literature accepts fragments or grains embedded in epoxy, nor does it specify acceptable grain sizes, fragment dimensions, or general quality requirements for such standards. It does, however, establish the key analytical requirement that standards and unknowns be properly prepared so that differences in measured x-ray intensity arise from composition rather than geometry. Surface roughness can produce substantial errors, particularly for low-energy x-rays. A Monte Carlo simulation of a crenellated FeO surface found that geometric effects remained at or above 5% for surface features about 100 nm high and laterally spaced, while polishing to a relief below 20 nm reduced the roughness contribution below 1% for O K and Fe L photons. Thus, the excerpt supports the importance of a very flat, well-polished exposed analytical surface, but it provides no evidence about epoxy mounting, minimum grain size, criteria for accepting fragments, or why large fragments would be preferred. contexts.context: This excerpt does not state whether EPMA standards literature accepts fragments or grains embedded in epoxy, nor does it specify acceptable standard grain sizes, fragment dimensions, or quality requirements. Its relevant point is that quantitative EPMA results are highly sensitive to the prepared surface and any compositionally altered or contaminated surface layer. Consequently, reference materials and analyzed specimens should be prepared using rigorously identical polishing procedures. The article also warns that surface composition can change during prolonged storage in air, recommending analysis immediately after polishing. The cited 0.25 µm dimension refers to diamond abrasive grains used in polishing, not to the required size of standard fragments. Likewise, the discussion of grain size concerns how abrasive wear affects cathodoluminescence in alumina, rather than establishing criteria for embedded EPMA standards. Therefore, this passage provides background on polishing consistency and surface stability but does not support conclusions about whether large fragments are preferred, what minimum grain size is required, or what physical quality standards embedded grains must meet.
contexts.question: Does EPMA standards literature accept fragments or grains embedded in epoxy and polished as standards? What grain sizes and quality requirements are stated, and why are large fragments preferred?

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specifically discuss whether grains or fragments embedded in epoxy are acceptable, nor does it identify epoxy mounting itself as a problem. It does, however, state the general quality criteria expected for EPMA standards: they should be homogeneous at the micron scale, well characterized, widely available, and compositionally similar to the samples being analyzed. Small master fragments are viewed as problematic because they generally cannot be independently characterized by techniques other than EPMA; their working compositions therefore depend on the accuracy of the microprobe analysis. The excerpt contrasts preferred large fragments with small grains, noting that commercial mounts should be produced from large fragments from well-stocked standard-material supplies, since users prefer approximately 1 mm chunks rather than 10 µm grains. Grain size alone is therefore not the sole acceptance criterion: a small grain could be usable if it is demonstrably homogeneous and well characterized, but undocumented origin, assumed composition, EPMA-only calibration, or multiphase intergrowth makes a standard deficient. The text also warns that multiphase or heterogeneous materials are unsuitable and emphasizes independent analytical pedigree, such as wet chemistry or NIST-related characterization.
contexts.question: Does EPMA standards literature accept fragments or grains embedded in epoxy and polished as standards? What grain sizes and quality requirements are stated, and why are large fragments preferred?

contexts.context: High-accuracy SEM-EDS k-ratio/matrix correction requires standards and unknowns to be measured under closely matched conditions: highly polished, unetched surfaces; the same beam energy, delivered dose (beam current and detector live time), beam-incidence angle, detector take-off angle, detector efficiency, and effectively constant detector-to-target geometry/solid angle. Surface topography is especially damaging for low-energy X-rays, so flat, smooth, metallographically prepared specimens are essential. The excerpt does not state a specific bulk-dimension requirement, but it emphasizes reproducible specimen positioning and warns that specimen geometry can severely affect accuracy regardless of whether standards-based or standardless analysis is used. Standards and analyzed regions should represent homogeneous material at the micrometer scale; the cited materials included specimens confirmed homogeneous laterally on that scale. Specimens should have highly polished, flat surfaces to suppress topographic and geometric effects; polishing must not be followed by chemical or electrochemical etching because it can alter the interrogated near-surface composition. contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that high-accuracy SEM/EDS quantification requires controlling specimen geometry rather than relying on automatic normalization. The example of NIST SRM 470 uses a microscopically homogeneous glass prepared as a flat, highly polished bulk specimen, with a final 100 nm alumina polish and a thin (<10 nm) carbon coating for charge dissipation. These conditions provide an ideal geometry for standards-based k-ratio analysis. Shape, specimen size, surface damage, voids, chips, shards, and local surface inclination alter electron scattering and the X-ray path length to the detector, thereby changing absorption and measured intensities. Consequently, specimens and standards need comparable, controlled geometry and surface condition for accurate k-ratio results; the excerpt specifically documents the ideal specimen preparation but does not state a numerical accuracy limit or explicitly detail all matching requirements. Violating these conditions can produce large, uncontrolled, and potentially unrecognized errors. Internal normalization to unity conceals the resulting analytical-total deviations, creating an appearance of accuracy while removing an important diagnostic of geometry-related error. The figures compare ideal bulk material with scratched, holed, chipped, and shard forms, illustrating that accuracy is substantially compromised when flatness, polish, bulk form, and geometry are not maintained.
contexts.question: What conditions do high-accuracy SEM-EDS k-ratio protocols impose on standards and specimens (flatness, polish, bulk dimensions, homogeneity, same conditions), and what accuracy is achievable or lost when these are violated?

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Is it accepted practice in SEM-EDS / electron microprobe analysis to prepare quantification standards by mounting high-purity metal powders or granules in epoxy and polishing cross-sections? How large must particles be relative to the electron interaction volume at 15-20 kV, and what artifacts limit accuracy compared with bulk polished standards (surface oxide films at particle boundaries, porosity, smearing of soft metals such as tin, edge effects)?

# Epoxy-mounted metal powders as SEM-EDS/EPMA standards

## Conclusion

**Yes—with qualifications.** Embedding high-purity metal grains or fragments in epoxy and polishing through them is an established and technically valid way to make a **working SEM-EDS or EPMA standard mount**. The epoxy itself is not disqualifying if the exposed metallic cross-section is flat, homogeneous, electrically grounded, and sufficiently large that the analyzed point behaves as a semi-infinite bulk specimen. Standards may be co-mounted or kept on a separate mount, and pure elements are acceptable k-ratio standards when their composition and surface condition are known. However, standards practice favors large, independently characterized fragments—approximately millimetre-sized material rather than 10-µm grains—and a mounted powder should not automatically be treated as metrologically equivalent to a certified bulk polished coupon. (carpenter2008epmastandardsthe pages 1-2, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 11-13, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2)

For high-accuracy work, both standard and unknown must be highly polished and unetched, homogeneous on the micrometre scale, and measured at the same beam energy, dose, incidence/take-off geometry, detector conditions, and preferably matched coating thickness. Under such controls, standards-based SEM-EDS can produce approximately 1–3% relative errors in favorable major-element cases and routinely target ±5% for major constituents; nonideal geometry can instead produce errors from tens of percent to nearly an order of magnitude. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 2-4, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 6-7, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 4-5)

## Required particle size

There is **no universal minimum diameter**. It depends on beam energy, atomic number, density, X-ray line, detector geometry, and whether secondary fluorescence matters. The Kanaya–Okayama electron-range estimate is

\[
R_{KO}(\mu\mathrm{m})=\frac{0.0276\,A\,E_0^{1.67}}{Z^{0.89}\rho},
\]

where \(A\) is atomic mass, \(Z\) atomic number, \(\rho\) density in g cm⁻³, and \(E_0\) beam energy in keV. It estimates maximum electron penetration, not the exact X-ray generation diameter. (humphreys2006simsinvestigationof pages 7-8)

Representative Kanaya–Okayama ranges calculated from that equation are:

| Metal | 15 kV | 20 kV |
|---|---:|---:|
| Al | ~2.9 µm | ~4.7 µm |
| Fe | ~1.1 µm | ~1.7 µm |
| Cu | ~1.0 µm | ~1.6 µm |
| Sn | ~1.4 µm | ~2.2 µm |
| Au | ~0.8 µm | ~1.3 µm |

These are approximate maximum-depth scales; the lateral and useful X-ray generation dimensions must be checked by Monte Carlo simulation for the actual material and lines. Published microanalysis guidance places the 20-keV interaction scale broadly around 1–5 µm and notes that primary X-ray production in bulk SEM-EDS commonly spans approximately 0.5–10 µm. (newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 2-3, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4)

A conservative practical criterion is therefore:

* use a polished metallic cross-section **at least 5–10 times the largest primary interaction dimension**;
* place the beam **at least 2–3 interaction-volume radii from every metal–epoxy boundary, pore, oxide rim, or neighboring particle**;
* at 15–20 kV, prefer exposed sections **≥20–50 µm across** for routine major-element standardization; larger is better, and approximately 1-mm fragments are preferable where available;
* regard **~10-µm particles as marginal, especially at 20 kV**, for low-density metals such as Al, for points not exactly centered, or where polishing has left only a shallow cap;
* verify adequacy experimentally by moving the beam toward the edge and by comparing 15- and 20-kV results. A stable central plateau is required.

The 5–10× rule is a conservative engineering recommendation rather than a formal universal standard. It is consistent with experiments that used 20–200 µm particles explicitly larger than the interaction volume and found that an ~80-µm particle was effectively flat only near its top center. Conventional matrix corrections did not remove errors caused by curvature, edge position, or altered absorption paths. (newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 3-4, newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 4-5, newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 5-6)

A second, longer length scale applies to **secondary X-ray fluorescence**, which can extend roughly 10–100 µm. Consequently, a 20–50 µm grain may be adequate for major-element k-ratios yet still be imperfect for trace analysis if adjacent particles, metal-filled resin, the mount, or oxide-rich boundaries contain interfering elements. (newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 6-8, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4)

## Accuracy-limiting artifacts

The main limitations and controls are summarized below.

| Artifact | Mechanism in an epoxy-mounted metal particle | Expected EDS/EPMA bias | Mitigation; comparison with bulk standard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Finite particle / edge effects | If the beam is too close to the particle–epoxy boundary, electrons and generated X-rays escape the metal, while backscattered electrons may excite the epoxy or neighboring material. Local edge slope also changes take-off angle and absorption path. | Reduced metal intensity, low analytical totals, apparent C/O or neighboring-element signal, and line-dependent errors—usually greatest for low-energy X-rays. Normalizing to 100% can hide the problem. (newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 1-2, newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 2-3, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25) | Use grains many times larger than the full interaction region; analyze only the broad, flat center, at least several interaction-volume radii from every visible boundary. Confirm by line scans or measurements at increasing edge distance. A large bulk polished standard effectively eliminates finite-size edges. |
| Native oxide shell at particle–epoxy boundary | Powder’s original external oxide becomes an internal rim around the polished metal cross-section; polishing may also form a new oxide film on the exposed face. Small grains have high oxide-to-metal volume and boundary ratios. | O signal and depressed apparent metal concentration if the interaction volume intersects the rim; beam-energy-dependent results; low-energy metal lines may be attenuated. Different oxide thicknesses on standard and unknown invalidate ideal k-ratio cancellation. (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 21-22, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 14-15, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 4-5) | Select coarse, freshly cleaned granules; measure well inside the metallic core; repolish immediately before use and store dry/inert where warranted. Map O and reject rim-affected grains. Bulk metal has far less boundary oxide per usable area, although its exposed face can still oxidize. |
| Pores, pull-out, and epoxy intrusion | Poor wetting, trapped air, particle packing, or grinding pull-out leaves voids and resin-filled fissures beside or beneath the apparent metal surface. | Loss of metal X-ray yield, C/O contribution, charging, abnormal continuum, low totals, and irreproducible results as the beam overlaps hidden resin or voids. Geometry and specimen-size defects can cause large concentration shifts. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 6-7, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6) | Vacuum-impregnate with low-viscosity epoxy, disperse particles rather than allowing contact, grind deeply enough to expose sound interiors, and reject grains showing pores in BSE imaging. Dense bulk standards largely avoid resin intrusion and pull-out. |
| Polishing relief, scratches, or rounded edges | Large hardness contrast between metal and epoxy produces differential wear; abrasive polishing may round particle margins, plough grooves, or leave scratches comparable to the X-ray generation depth. | Changed electron scattering and X-ray escape paths; strongly absorbed low-energy lines may vary by several percent to orders of magnitude. Even residual scratches can create outlying analyses. (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 7-9, newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 3-4, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 6-7, newbury2013quantitativesemedsstep pages 1-2) | Use rigid, low-nap cloths, light loads, progressively fine abrasives, and a suitable final polish; verify flatness by SE/BSE imaging and avoid all relief and scratches. Bulk pieces are easier to polish coplanar and provide much larger relief-free areas. |
| Smearing / plastic flow of soft Sn | Tin deforms and ploughs rather than cutting cleanly; polishing can drag Sn across epoxy, pores, oxide rims, or adjacent standards and can fold altered surface material over the exposed core. | Locally elevated Sn outside the grain; variable Sn/O/C within it; concealed pores or oxide; an unrepresentative mechanically worked surface and poor repeatability. Micro-ploughing and wear-debris transfer are recognized preparation artifacts. (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 21-22, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 3-4) | Use minimal force and heat, sharp fine abrasives, short polishing times, rigid support, and a validated Sn-specific metallographic procedure; clean between stages and inspect maps for Sn tails. A larger bulk Sn coupon is better supported but remains susceptible to smearing. |
| Contamination or embedded abrasive | Diamond, alumina, colloidal silica, lubricant, wear debris, or metal transferred from neighboring standards can lodge in scratches, pores, or the soft metal surface. | Spurious C, O, Al, Si, or neighboring-metal peaks; diluted metal concentration; heterogeneous spot results. Polishing discs contaminated by wear debris can transfer reaction products or material between phases. (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 21-22, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 19-21, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 12-14) | Use dedicated clean consumables, thorough ultrasonic or solvent cleaning where chemically safe, and separate polishing of easily cross-contaminating metals. Screen by maps and reject inclusions. Bulk standards reduce boundary trapping but still require contamination control. |
| Poor electrical grounding / unequal coating | Isolated metal grains may not contact the conductive mount because epoxy surrounds them; charging changes landing energy and beam position. A carbon or metal coating also absorbs X-rays if its thickness differs between standard and unknown. | Count-rate instability, peak shifts, beam drift, altered effective overvoltage, and systematic low-energy-line errors; unequal coating thickness prevents cancellation in the k-ratio. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 2-4, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 11-13, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 4-5) | Provide a conductive path with carbon paint or a metal-filled mounting route where appropriate; coat standard and unknown together or to matched, monitored thickness. Bulk metal is readily grounded and often needs no coating. |
| Secondary fluorescence / remote excitation | Characteristic or continuum X-rays and backscattered electrons can excite adjacent particles, mounting hardware, or epoxy additives outside the primary electron interaction volume; the fluorescence range can reach tens of micrometres. | False trace/minor peaks or elevated intensities from nearby materials even when the primary interaction volume remains inside the target grain. Bulk-specimen guidance gives typical secondary-fluorescence dimensions of roughly 10–100 µm. (newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 6-8, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4) | Space grains and unlike standards widely, avoid metal-filled epoxy unless modeled, analyze central regions, and check suspect elements against blank epoxy and isolated grains. A large isolated bulk standard minimizes neighboring-material fluorescence but does not eliminate chamber or holder contributions. |


*Table: Preparation and geometry artifacts that can bias quantitative SEM-EDS or EPMA of epoxy-mounted pure-metal particles, with practical controls and the advantages of bulk polished standards.*

### Surface oxide films

Powders have much more original surface area than bulk coupons. Their native oxide becomes a circumferential internal rim when the grain is sectioned, while polishing and subsequent air exposure can create a new altered film on the exposed face. Polishing-induced metal oxides can range from a few nanometres to hundreds of nanometres. If the interaction volume intersects an oxide rim, the result contains O, gives depressed metal intensity, and no longer represents the nominal pure metal. Differences in native-oxide thickness between standard and unknown also defeat ideal k-ratio cancellation. (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 21-22, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 14-15, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 4-5)

A nanometre-scale oxide on the central face may have little effect at 15–20 kV for hard metal K lines, but it can matter for oxygen measurement and low-energy metal L/M lines. A micrometre-scale oxidized particle boundary is unacceptable if sampled. Use coarse freshly cleaned granules, map O, analyze only the metallic core, repolish shortly before use, and store oxidation-sensitive standards dry or inert.

### Porosity, pull-out, and epoxy intrusion

Entrapped air, inadequate resin infiltration, agglomerated powder, or grinding pull-out can leave resin-filled pores or subsurface voids. These reduce metal X-ray production, add C/O, alter the continuum, cause charging, and can produce low totals even when the surface appears metallic. Shape, holes, chips, shards, and voids are documented causes of large and scattered SEM-EDS errors. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 6-7, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6)

Vacuum impregnation with low-viscosity epoxy, widely separated grains, sufficiently deep sectioning, and BSE inspection are necessary. Reject any particle whose central analytical region contains pores, cracks, resin tongues, or pull-out.

### Relief, scratches, and particle edges

The metal–epoxy hardness contrast promotes differential polishing relief and rounded margins. Local slope changes electron backscattering, detector take-off angle, and X-ray absorption path. Effects are strongest for soft X-rays: rough Cu–Au surfaces produced Cu-L/Cu-K errors from −92% to +42%, and even ~100-nm relief can affect O-K and Fe-L intensities by at least 5%. Relief below approximately 20 nm reduced the modeled contribution below 1%; rigorous practical guidance calls for roughly 50-nm-rms or better surfaces for low-energy analysis. (newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 3-4, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 11-13, newbury2013quantitativesemedsstep pages 1-2)

Near a particle edge, electrons can leave the metal and excite epoxy or nearby phases, and X-rays may experience abnormal escape or absorption paths. Remote excitation by backscattered electrons may also generate apparently real minor or trace peaks outside the intended interaction region. Conventional ZAF or φ(ρz) corrections assume flat bulk geometry and do not correct these effects automatically. (newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 1-2, newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 11-12, newbury2006quantitativeelectronprobe pages 6-8)

### Smearing of soft metals, especially tin

Sn is mechanically soft and prone to plastic flow. Under excessive load or a compliant cloth it can plough and smear rather than cut cleanly, dragging Sn across epoxy, oxide rims, pores, or adjacent standards and folding altered material over the metallic core. The general polishing literature documents micro-ploughing, wear-debris transfer, and disproportionate deformation of soft phases; these mechanisms directly explain the familiar Sn-preparation problem, although the cited evidence does not establish a universal numerical Sn error. (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 21-22, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 3-4)

Use rigid low-nap support, low force and heat, fresh sharp fine abrasive, short polishing steps, thorough cleaning between stages, and an Sn-validated metallographic procedure. Inspect Sn and O maps for tails or films outside the nominal grain. A bulk Sn coupon is better supported and offers a larger clean area, but it too can smear.

## Recommended acceptance test

An epoxy-mounted granular standard should be accepted only after it passes the following checks:

1. **Pedigree:** documented purity and impurity inventory, preferably independently characterized rather than assigned solely by EDS/EPMA. High nominal purity does not establish homogeneity or absence of oxide. (carpenter2008epmastandardsthe pages 1-2, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2)
2. **Geometry:** a flat, unetched central area ≥5–10 interaction dimensions across, with no edge, pore, crack, or second phase within at least 2–3 interaction radii.
3. **Preparation:** minimal relief and scratches; matched conductive coating and reliable grounding. Standards and unknowns should be prepared and measured comparably. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 2-4, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 11-13)
4. **Imaging/maps:** BSE plus O, C, and target-metal maps to identify oxide rims, epoxy intrusion, polishing debris, and smearing.
5. **Repeatability:** multiple central points on several particles should agree within counting statistics and the laboratory’s control limits. Do not normalize away poor analytical totals; totals are a diagnostic for geometry and contamination. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6)
6. **Voltage/edge test:** compare central results at 15 and 20 kV and acquire an edge-distance profile. Systematic voltage dependence or drift toward the edge indicates finite size, oxide, porosity, or layered-surface effects.
7. **Traceability:** compare the mounted-particle standard against a validated bulk polished standard. If major-element ratios differ by more than the intended uncertainty—typically a few percent for rigorous standards-based work—the granular mount should be treated only as qualitative or semiquantitative. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 2-4, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 4-5)

Thus, **coarse epoxy-mounted granules are accepted as practical working standards when validated**, but fine powders are a compromise. For the most accurate EPMA/SEM-EDS calibration—particularly low-energy lines, oxygen, trace constituents, or interlaboratory work—large, dense, polished bulk standards remain preferable because they provide much more edge-free area and reduce oxide-boundary, porosity, resin, relief, grounding, and secondary-fluorescence artifacts.

artifacts.artifact-00:
| Artifact | Mechanism in an epoxy-mounted metal particle | Expected EDS/EPMA bias | Mitigation; comparison with bulk standard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Finite particle / edge effects | If the beam is too close to the particle–epoxy boundary, electrons and generated X-rays escape the metal, while backscattered electrons may excite the epoxy or neighboring material. Local edge slope also changes take-off angle and absorption path. | Reduced metal intensity, low analytical totals, apparent C/O or neighboring-element signal, and line-dependent errors—usually greatest for low-energy X-rays. Normalizing to 100% can hide the problem. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000024) | Use grains many times larger than the full interaction region; analyze only the broad, flat center, at least several interaction-volume radii from every visible boundary. Confirm by line scans or measurements at increasing edge distance. A large bulk polished standard effectively eliminates finite-size edges. |
| Native oxide shell at particle–epoxy boundary | Powder’s original external oxide becomes an internal rim around the polished metal cross-section; polishing may also form a new oxide film on the exposed face. Small grains have high oxide-to-metal volume and boundary ratios. | O signal and depressed apparent metal concentration if the interaction volume intersects the rim; beam-energy-dependent results; low-energy metal lines may be attenuated. Different oxide thicknesses on standard and unknown invalidate ideal k-ratio cancellation. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027) | Select coarse, freshly cleaned granules; measure well inside the metallic core; repolish immediately before use and store dry/inert where warranted. Map O and reject rim-affected grains. Bulk metal has far less boundary oxide per usable area, although its exposed face can still oxidize. |
| Pores, pull-out, and epoxy intrusion | Poor wetting, trapped air, particle packing, or grinding pull-out leaves voids and resin-filled fissures beside or beneath the apparent metal surface. | Loss of metal X-ray yield, C/O contribution, charging, abnormal continuum, low totals, and irreproducible results as the beam overlaps hidden resin or voids. Geometry and specimen-size defects can cause large concentration shifts. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) | Vacuum-impregnate with low-viscosity epoxy, disperse particles rather than allowing contact, grind deeply enough to expose sound interiors, and reject grains showing pores in BSE imaging. Dense bulk standards largely avoid resin intrusion and pull-out. |
| Polishing relief, scratches, or rounded edges | Large hardness contrast between metal and epoxy produces differential wear; abrasive polishing may round particle margins, plough grooves, or leave scratches comparable to the X-ray generation depth. | Changed electron scattering and X-ray escape paths; strongly absorbed low-energy lines may vary by several percent to orders of magnitude. Even residual scratches can create outlying analyses. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | Use rigid, low-nap cloths, light loads, progressively fine abrasives, and a suitable final polish; verify flatness by SE/BSE imaging and avoid all relief and scratches. Bulk pieces are easier to polish coplanar and provide much larger relief-free areas. |
| Smearing / plastic flow of soft Sn | Tin deforms and ploughs rather than cutting cleanly; polishing can drag Sn across epoxy, pores, oxide rims, or adjacent standards and can fold altered surface material over the exposed core. | Locally elevated Sn outside the grain; variable Sn/O/C within it; concealed pores or oxide; an unrepresentative mechanically worked surface and poor repeatability. Micro-ploughing and wear-debris transfer are recognized preparation artifacts. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000015) | Use minimal force and heat, sharp fine abrasives, short polishing times, rigid support, and a validated Sn-specific metallographic procedure; clean between stages and inspect maps for Sn tails. A larger bulk Sn coupon is better supported but remains susceptible to smearing. |
| Contamination or embedded abrasive | Diamond, alumina, colloidal silica, lubricant, wear debris, or metal transferred from neighboring standards can lodge in scratches, pores, or the soft metal surface. | Spurious C, O, Al, Si, or neighboring-metal peaks; diluted metal concentration; heterogeneous spot results. Polishing discs contaminated by wear debris can transfer reaction products or material between phases. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014) | Use dedicated clean consumables, thorough ultrasonic or solvent cleaning where chemically safe, and separate polishing of easily cross-contaminating metals. Screen by maps and reject inclusions. Bulk standards reduce boundary trapping but still require contamination control. |
| Poor electrical grounding / unequal coating | Isolated metal grains may not contact the conductive mount because epoxy surrounds them; charging changes landing energy and beam position. A carbon or metal coating also absorbs X-rays if its thickness differs between standard and unknown. | Count-rate instability, peak shifts, beam drift, altered effective overvoltage, and systematic low-energy-line errors; unequal coating thickness prevents cancellation in the k-ratio. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000027) | Provide a conductive path with carbon paint or a metal-filled mounting route where appropriate; coat standard and unknown together or to matched, monitored thickness. Bulk metal is readily grounded and often needs no coating. |
| Secondary fluorescence / remote excitation | Characteristic or continuum X-rays and backscattered electrons can excite adjacent particles, mounting hardware, or epoxy additives outside the primary electron interaction volume; the fluorescence range can reach tens of micrometres. | False trace/minor peaks or elevated intensities from nearby materials even when the primary interaction volume remains inside the target grain. Bulk-specimen guidance gives typical secondary-fluorescence dimensions of roughly 10–100 µm. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000019) | Space grains and unlike standards widely, avoid metal-filled epoxy unless modeled, analyze central regions, and check suspect elements against blank epoxy and isolated grains. A large isolated bulk standard minimizes neighboring-material fluorescence but does not eliminate chamber or holder contributions. |


*Table: Preparation and geometry artifacts that can bias quantitative SEM-EDS or EPMA of epoxy-mounted pure-metal particles, with practical controls and the advantages of bulk polished standards.*

info.query: Is it accepted practice in SEM-EDS / electron microprobe analysis to prepare quantification standards by mounting high-purity metal powders or granules in epoxy and polishing cross-sections? How large must particles be relative to the electron interaction volume at 15-20 kV, and what artifacts limit accuracy compared with bulk polished standards (surface oxide films at particle boundaries, porosity, smearing of soft metals such as tin, edge effects)?
